Annotated Bibliography 
This task must be carried out in your allocated ACF100 project group.  Project groups will be 
allocated during week 3. If you join the course after the project groups are allocated, it is your 
responsibility to find out which group you have been allocated to by contacting the Student Support 
Assistant (Rowan Hall, r.hall6@lancaster.ac.uk).  
  
 2 
 
1. The task 
Each group is required to produce an annotated bibliography on a chosen issue from the list 
provided below in section 2. The aim of the annotated bibliography is not to provide comprehensive 
coverage or evaluation of a topic/issue but, as a group, to identify and clearly and concisely discuss 
useful and relevant source materials relating to the issue. The group is restricted to including one 
source material per member. It is important that the sources used should be presented to put 
forward a viewpoint on the issue that is supported by evidence from the source materials. 
Therefore, the group should consider carefully and agree upon which are the most appropriate 
source materials to include. 
1.1. What is an annotated bibliography? 
It is helpful to break the phrase ‘annotated bibliography’ down as follows: 
 Bibliography => a list of sources 
 Annotation => notes explaining something 
Therefore: 
An annotated bibliography is a collection of the sources you have used to research a particular topic, 
with brief explanations or notes which: 
 Describe the sources’ content. 
 Summarises the main argument. 
 And sometimes briefly analyses the source itself. 
Please see link to moodle for further information about the purpose of an annotated bibliography 
along with some examples.  
1.2. What should be included in the annotated bibliography? 
The annotated bibliography has to include: 
a. A title page including the names of all team members. 
b. A brief introduction outlining the chosen issue (including any necessary background). 
c. Discussion of various source materials, one by one.   
d. A conclusion which summarises the main arguments in your readings.   
e. A reference list (which is the bibliography element). 
f. An appendix containing the group contribution sheet. 
1.3. The requirement 
Each group member should pick one source material item to write about and he/she will be 
responsible for writing the discussion piece (the ‘annotations’) on this particular item for this section  3 
 
of the annotated bibliography. Each source material item should be discussed in a subsection of 
between a minimum of 100 and a maximum of 300 words (between one and three paragraphs). In 
this discussion you should address the following for each source material item: 
(i) topic coverage of the issue (i.e. what the source material item actually tells the reader about 
the topic area chosen or what aspects of the issue are addressed); 
(ii) the writer’s viewpoint/argument/conclusions;  
(iii) how useful the piece is in terms of the information provided (i.e. how relevant is the piece 
and how much information is conveyed) and what evidence is put forward to support the 
writer’s viewpoint; and  
(iv) how this extends or contradicts views put forward in source material items selected by other 
members of the group. 
The group should include at least one item of all of the following source types in their overall 
portfolio of sources: 
SOURCE TYPE 1: Academic journal article 
SOURCE TYPE 2: Book or book extract or book chapter or report 
SOURCE TYPE 3: High quality newspaper or magazine or periodical article 
SOURCE TYPE 4: Webpage  
Examples of these source types are included in section 9 of this document. 
If there are more than four team members in the group, it is up to the group which source type is 
included twice (no source type should be referred to more than twice).  
Each of the source materials should also be referenced fully in the reference list at the end of the 
annotated bibliography.  The reference list should appear in alphabetical order by the author’s 
surname (for sources that have more than one author, the first named author’s surname determines 
the alphabetical order in the reference list). PLEASE NOTE: You should find new source materials for 
this task, i.e. materials included should not be contained in the course reading list. 
1.4. Word limit  
The length of your annotated bibliography will depend upon the number of members in your group.  
The introduction and concluding sections should in total be no more than 500 words long. It is 
recommended that each is approximately 250 words. 
The discussion for each source material item should be a minimum of 100 words and a maximum 
of 300 words. Please note: one source material item per group member is required and each 
member is responsible for his/her piece – groups will be penalised if any members do not select and 
comment on their selected item. In addition, although this is a group effort, it is important that the 
finished piece hangs together properly as a single document, and is consistent in style and format 
throughout. It is useful to make one person responsible for this task. See below suggestions for 
group organisation in section 4.  4 
 
Please note: the Module Director is unable to provide feedback on the choice of sources and/or the 
annotated bibliography in advance of the coursework submission date.  
1.5. Deadline 
The deadline is Wednesday 23rd November 2022 at 12 noon (UK time).  Please note: late mark 
penalties will be applied if your group’s annotated bibliography is not submitted by this deadline.  
All submissions must also contain the contribution sheet as an Appendix (please download the 
template from Moodle). Please ensure the names of all team members are included in your 
annotated bibliography. Only ONE copy per group is required for submission. Therefore, please 
allocate someone in your team the task of uploading the PDF document on Moodle prior to the 
deadline. 
Please note: The Department reserves the right to adjust coursework marks after coursework has 
been returned to students in order to ensure that the coursework marks have an appropriate 
distribution. 
1.6. How and where to submit your assignment 
Your annotated bibliography must submitted online in a PDF file via the AcF100 Moodle site. The 
submission folder is contained within the ‘Assessments and assessment guidance’ section. Please 
note that the folder will not become visible to you until the end of week 6 to encourage you to work 
on this together over a three week period.  
   5 
 
2. Topic areas 
The group should choose ONE topic from the list below:  
a. The impact which technology has upon the accounting profession. 
Note that accounting profession means accountants in the broadest sense so could include 
financial accountants, management accountants, tax experts, actuaries amongst others.  
b. The risks and opportunities for the accounting profession arising from global events for 
example Covid-19 or Brexit. 
Note that Covid-19 or Brexit are purely examples and other global events are equally as 
relevant. 
c. The importance for an organisation’s performance of having a diverse workforce (including 
diversity among senior executives).  
d. The main threats posed to the accounting profession from high-profile audit failures?  
It is entirely up to the group which topic is chosen and the same marks are available for each of the 
topic areas.  The marking criteria is detailed further in section 6 of this document. 
   6 
 
3. Formatting of your annotated bibliography 
Your annotated bibliography should be word-processed with 1.5 line spacing. An appropriate font 
size to use is Arial or Times New Roman size 12 (or similar) for the main body text.  You may wish to 
enlarge the font size used for any headings/title of your piece. The sections/subsections should be 
clearly titled. You should also clearly label any charts, tables or diagrams (and identify the source of 
information) used in your annotated bibliography, if you decide to include any of these. To help the 
marker, you may also wish to leave a line between each paragraph and indent the start of each 
paragraph. 
 
You should include a title page which includes the names and student ID numbers of team members. 
Ensure all pages are correctly numbered and include a word count at the end of the document.  
 
Please note: The reference list is not included in the word count, but citations within the text are 
included in the word count (not headings). There is no 10% allowance in the word count and if you 
go over the word limit, it is at the marker’s discretion as to whether you will be penalised for this. 
 
A common mistake is to report on everything. This is not necessary or effective! It is important to 
focus on the key issues. Additional material should be placed in an appendix, but be selective in this. 
If you do decide to include material in an appendix, it is important to refer to this in the main text of 
your annotated bibliography (Note: the appendix is not usually included within the word count, but 
it should not be seen as a dumping ground for material exceeding the word limit.).

4. Group organisation 
4.1. Groups  
At the end of Week 3 you will be allocated to your group. An announcement will be released using 
ACF100 Moodle – please note your group will be formed of other members of your workshop, this 
will help you make friends within your workshop itself.  
Once your groups are released I would strongly recommend immediately arranging when to meet up 
so you can start working on the task. There are plenty of places on campus and in the Management 
School where you could meet up. Whilst you can speak with your group mates in your workshop, I 
will also set up some groups on Microsoft Teams so you can also speak with each other on there if 
you choose. Things you will want to do in the first meeting include: 
 Introducing yourself to your group mates. 
 Discussing the task. 
 Reviewing written versions of draft documents. 
 Documenting minutes for each meeting. 
4.2. Team roles 
It is up to you how you decide to arrange the various team roles. It is recommended that you elect 
the following roles: 
 Chair (someone who has an overview role for the whole project and ensures everything is 
completed by the deadline).   
 Editor (someone who can review the annotated bibliography after the writing is complete 
for consistency and coherence, and make necessary suggestions to individual group 
members for stylistic changes to their individual contributions to ensure coherence, and 
ensures consistency with the introduction and conclusion) 
 Secretary (someone to take team meeting minutes) 
Your group is required to keep a record of progress throughout the term through meeting minutes.  
Guidance is provided below for arranging meetings and writing meeting minutes. 
4.3. Arranging meetings & meeting minutes 
4.3.1. Arranging meetings 
In arranging a meeting, students should pay careful consideration to any of their team members who 
do not live on campus and ensure that they arrange a mutually convenient time to meet. What may 
be a convenient time for one member of the group may be very inconvenient for another.  
At a minimum it is recommended that you have meetings as follows: 
 Week 4 => introductions, allocating team roles and allocating sources.  8 
 
 Week 5 => progress meeting and review any work completed to date. 
 Week 6 => progress meeting. Note that at this stage you should almost have completed your 
individual elements. 
 Week 7 => final review of the report and agreement for submission. 
4.3.2. Sending apologies 
It is the group’s responsibility to arrange group meetings. Anyone who is going to be absent from a 
meeting should send their apologies to the group chair or secretary. Apologies should be sent using 
the chat in Teams. It is expected that students will attend group meetings unless there are 
exceptional circumstances which prevent them from doing so.  
4.3.3. Writing an agenda 
When arranging the meeting, an agenda of items for discussion should be agreed and circulated to 
all team members in advance. This gives people the chance to prepare for the meeting and should 
be used as the basis for discussion. 
4.3.4. Meeting minutes 
Each group should keep a record of the meeting minutes from each meeting. The minutes should 
contain the following: 
 Time, date and venue of the meeting 
 List of people attending 
 List of people absent from the meeting 
 Approval of previous minutes from meetings and any matters arising from the minutes 
 For each item on the agenda, a record of the main points discussed and the conclusion of 
the discussion.  
 Record any action points (i.e. work tasks) arising from the discussion and who is going to 
take responsibility for them. 
 Time, date and venue of the next meeting 
 Name of person taking the minutes 
After the meeting the minutes should be written up and circulated to all team members.  
Tip: Keep the minutes short and to the point. It is not necessary to have a word-for-word account of 
what was said, just a summary of the main points and any action points agreed. Write these as soon 
as you can after the meeting when they are fresh in your mind.

5. Monitoring contribution & resolving team difficulties 
Employers often tell us that the reason they like Lancaster University graduates is their experience of 
undertaking group work during their university course. We believe that this is a very important skill 
for students to practise on the AcF 100 course. However, we acknowledge that on occasion there 
may be problems within a group and it is important in group work to ensure everyone is making 
their contribution.   
5.1. Monitoring Contribution 
To ensure that all students contribute equitably to the project, each group will be required to 
complete a project group contribution sheet listing the actual tasks and contribution made by each 
group member. It is therefore important that each group keeps a rough journal of its process and 
this will be assisted by the meeting minutes which the group should prepare after each meeting.  
The chair should fill in the group contribution sheet in consultation with his/her project team. The 
form contains sections where the individual contribution towards the various tasks is highlighted.  
Where a person has not been contributing, this should also be highlighted. The contribution sheet 
should be agreed by all team members. An example of the contribution sheet is included at the end 
of this document. The contribution sheet will be available to download from Moodle. 
Reviews of individual contributions towards the task will be carried out by the course director and 
tutor.  
Please Note: If it emerges that individual team members have not made an equitable contribution, 
your tutor in conjunction with the course director have the power to take action against non-
contributing members, including reducing their individual marks. We will only use evidence through 
meeting minutes and the group contribution sheet so it is vital that groups record the discussions 
and outcomes. 
5.2. Resolving Team Difficulties 
If the group is experiencing problems during the term, you should first meet up and try and resolve 
the issues within the group in the first instance. If this is not possible, then the team (or an 
individual team member) should contact the course contact (Andrew) during his advertised office 
hours to discuss the issue. However you must be able to demonstrate that you have attempted to 
resolve the issue. 
Also note, that group mates should not make unilateral decisions to exclude an individual team 
member from the group. This can often cause as many difficulties as a group member not engaging 
with the task.

10. SELF-HELP CHECKLIST  
This section should be reviewed by the group prior to the submission of the annotated bibliography. 
This section provides guidance on: (i) document formatting, (ii) document structure and 
argumentation, (iii) writing style, appropriateness and accuracy of language, and (iv) referencing 
conventions. Active web-links are available below to additional study skills resources that may help 
the group in preparing/checking their annotated bibliography prior to submission. 
10.1. Format  
 Does the cover sheet have all necessary information included? Is the exact title of the 
question included? 
 Are the font and spacing clear and legible? 
 Does it follow the specifications for word count/number of pages? 
10.2. Structure and argumentation 
 Is there a helpful introduction? 
 Is effective reasoning used? (Do you support points with explanations, illustrations, 
justifications, evidence?)  
 Are headings/subheadings helpful and sufficient? 
 Are the points in logical order? 
 Does the paragraphing help the reader understand the argument and flow of ideas?   
 Is there one topic per paragraph? (there should be no one-sentence paragraphs)   
 Are there clear breaks between paragraphs to show where they start and end? 
 Is it clear how the ideas link together? (both within and between paragraphs) 
10.3. Style, appropriateness and accuracy of language 
 Is a formal style used, including full paragraphs (not notes or bullet points)?  
 Is it clear and easy to follow (not too cryptic or overcomplicated)? 
 Is English grammar used accurately e.g. tenses, word endings etc. 
 Is the punctuation clear and accurate e.g. full stops, commas, semi-colons? 
 Is the spelling accurate? 
 Have the spelling and grammar tools from Microsoft Word been used to double-check? 
10.4. Referencing conventions: 
 Are citations given in the text for all the source material used? See LUMS Reference Guide (self-
enrol on Moodle to access resource). 
 Are direct quotations given in quotation marks with surname, date and page number where 
available? Are paraphrases and quotations used appropriately (e.g. not too much 
quotation)? 
 Are sources which the student has read for her/himself acknowledged clearly with surname and 
date of the source? 
 Are indirect sources - ones the students has not read him/herself but has seen mentioned by  17 
 
other writers - acknowledged properly, giving the original source? E.g. (Kim and Lim 2003 cited in 
Brown 2004). 
 Are websites cited in the text concisely (i.e. author/organisation and date only)? 
 Are all the sources acknowledged within the text also included in the reference list at the end? 
 Are the references in alphabetical order of surname (of first named author for references with 
multiple authors), with the surname first followed by the initial(s)? For books, are all the details 
included? (author, year, title, place of publication and publisher.) 
  For journal articles, are all the details included? (author(s), year, title of article, journal name, 
volume/issue number, page range.)  
 Are journal titles and book titles given in italics? 
 For electronic sources, are all the details included? (author/organisation, date, full URL and date 
accessed)

It allows employees to provide rich and variedinformation to their teams, expand the scope of their operations, effectively account for feedbackfrom the market and increase the scale of production. Shortages and the nature of the toilet paper industry  
A toilet paper shortage occurred during COVID -19. The demand for toilet paper had exceeded the supply 
of it. People were starting to increase the time of staying at home, which means that the demand of using 
toilet paper would be also raised. However, this is not the exclusive reason of toilet paper shortage. The 
other reason is panic buying. Since the majority stayed at home, they felt anxious causing hysteria as shelves 
were empty. 
“Stock cannot be supplemented timely” is a fact. There are some natures of toilet paper supply chain. Firstly, 
according to the article posted by Willy Shih on Forbes, toilet paper has low value density, because toilet 
paper is lightweight but  is shipped in large volumes . The price of toilet paper is less than the cost of its 
transport. To save the cost, producers have domestic manufacturing to short en the distance of shipment. 
Secondly, Willy Shih (2020) also said that people have a stable demand for toilet paper.  The quantity of 
consumption of toilet paper in a region depends on the size of the population. The producers will produce 
based on the consumption pattern and will not produce more the increase the inventory, since the producers 
must increase the expenditure on storing the redundant products. Thirdly, the shipment of raw materials – 
wood fibre is long distance as the wood fibre comes from trees in the countries in the southern hemisphere. 
Due to the stable demand and long distance of shipment of raw material, producers also do not store extra 
raw material. Moreover, according to Lora Cecere (2021), the toilet paper industry commonly has multiple 
distribution channels, and toilet paper producers cannot im mediately receive the signal to increase 
production. 
There are 4 competitive priorities: Cost, Quality, Time, and Flexibility. Cost is one of the common 
competitions between brands. Brands can reduce the cost of a product to decrease the price of product, 
which means that they can compete with other brands. There are three ways to decrease the cost: costs of 
the raw materials, cost of shipment and cost of distribution channels. Taking Andrex toilet paper as an 
example: in Andrex official website, the detail page of Andrex classic clean toilet tissue (n.d.) is showing 
that the quantity of each roll has been increased 50% so that it can directly decrease shipment cost. Quality 
is the base of a product. It is the main consideration of some customers to choose which brand of products. 
Using Andrex classic clean  toilet tissue again, it is introduced that it is used unique 3D wave technique 
which can have better clean with fewer sheets. It can be an effective competition point comparing with 
other goods. flexibility is a method to stabilize current market share or improve competitive advantages for 
new market share. It means that the flexibility of a product can flexibly satisfy demands of different groups 
of customers. For instance, Andrex classic clean toilet tissue (n.d.) is packaged using 30% recycled plastics. 
It can be attractive for the customers who think the environment is important, which is a good selling point 
for a specific group. Finally, Shipping time is “Time” in 4 competition priorities. Shops or retailers would 
not have any supply shortages if the shipment time is short. It is significantly important that timely 
supplements and delivery would not affect the profits of what retailers or shops can get. It means that 
retailers and shops would be willing to stock the products which have short shipping t ime. However, it is 
unachievable in toilet paper industry because of high shipment cost. Therefore, the industry should 
concentrate on 3 competitive priorities – cost, quality, and flexibility – to ensure the competitiveness in this 
huge market.  
 
Why shortages occurred and were prolonged.     
 
   
 
The nature of the product irrefutably prolonged and caused the shortage. Toilet paper itself is a good which 
is inexpensive yet lightweight and voluminous. As a result, it has a low value density (Shih, W 2020). An 
example of a good with a high value densi ty is something like gold. Due to th is property, it is not very 
tradeable across countries. Countries are self -sufficient in producing their own toilet paper due to this. It 
reduces the cost and demand to ship toilet paper. However, due to this, supermarkets were not able to keep 
up with demand. The relative cost of toilet paper is far lower than the cost of shipping and transporting it 
long distances. Therefore, during the shortage, it a main reason that it was prolonged is the nature of the 
product as it is not worth being shipped across countries due to its low value density. A lack of shipping 
capability led to the shortage being prolonged as demand could not be satisfied this way. 
The supply chain has 4 primary cycles within it. The customer order cycle, the replenishment cycle, 
manufacturing cycle and the procurement cycle. Due to the increase in demand, these cycles deviate from 
their original values. For example, the customer ord er cycle becomes larger as more people are ordering. 
The replenishment cycle occurs more often as they find it harder to meet demand. The manufacturing cycle 
becomes larger as they must produce more and so does the procurement cycle as they need more suppl ies. 
This disrupts the supply chain. It becomes more difficult to manage due to more uncertainty. Suppliers were 
therefore limited in their actions to overcome this prolonging the impact of the toilet paper shortage. 
However, it could be argued that that is also due to the nature of the good. Demand is constant as toilet 
paper is a functional good. As a result, when demand shifted upwards so suddenly, manufacturers went out 
of stock too quickly and manufacturers didn’t have ample time to respond. The reason demand has shifted 
so far was due to the properties of toilet paper. It is inexpensive and considered to be an essential good. As 
a result, it was susceptible to panic buying caused by the pandemic. It was further pr olonged due to the 
variability of demand. With the variability of demand, it became harder for supply chains to predict demand 
and meet it, causing shortages to occur. Furthermore, stores only keep several weeks of stock in hand, which 
is partially responsible for the initial shortage. 
The lack of capacity of the suppliers and manufacturers in the supply chain was also responsible for the 
shortage. As mentioned before, demand for toilet paper is usually stable, therefore, manufacturers and 
suppliers do not have large amounts of spare cap acity as capacity utilization is quite high. Due to the lack 
cushion capacity, the excess demand was not met as quickly as it could have been thus prolonging the 
shortage. Furthermore, even if they were to try to increase their capacity, they would be met with 
difficulties. The factors of production are inelastic, meaning that even if the demand was to go up for toilet 
paper, it would take too long for them to increase their factors of production to meet it. For example, 
specialized machines for only home use and not commercial use are expensive and take a long tim e to 
receive the machinery (Cecere, L 2021). The characteristics and shortcomings of the supply chain itself did 
play a part in the shortage. 
In conclusion, it w as due to both the nature of toilet paper and the design of the supply chain. It was a 
culmination of these 2 factors which caused the shortage to occur and to be prolonged. 
 
Demand shock, shortages and the bullwhip effect 
During covid-19, the bullwhip effect occurred as toilet paper is not a seasonal consumer item, and toilet 
paper is something that has a steady demand in the market. During covid, the bullwhip effect was large. In 
normal times, manufacturers and suppliers can predict market demand more accurately. However, during 
covid-19, customers were buying and hoarding toilet paper, breaking the balance of supply and demand.  
There are many other important parts from the manufacturer to the final purchaser to form a comp lete     
 
   
 
supply chain. The manufacturer estimates the supply of the production platform from the changes in the 
market, and each part will set up a safe storage capacity to minimize and avoid losses caused by product 
shortages. The huge demand shock and the shortage of goods have caused a lot of increase in the estimates 
of market demand by distributors and manufacturers, which has also led to manufacturers getting incorrect 
information. Manufacturers will speed up production to ensure that the crisis will reduce product shortages. 
At the same time, as the crisis passed, consumers hoarded a large amount of inventory, and it took them a 
while to get through, which meant that the storage cost of suppliers increased. This can lead to backlogs in 
stores and signal production cuts.  
To solve this kind of problem, Professor Hau Lee produced a very good solution, he creates a kind of supply 
chain call triple a supply chain, Hau Lee says, a highly aligned and agile supply chain can ensure that 
manufacturers can cope with large demand shocks and product shortages in the short term.  
 
Agility 
1. It can promote the synchronous flow of real -time information among supply chain partners, so that 
suppliers and manufacturers do not need to estimate market demand due to special impacts caused by 
special circumstances. 
2. Develop a reliable logistics system or partners. A reliable logistics system can effectively reduce 
transportation costs, so that enterprises can make better profits. If they have an independent logistics 
system, they can respond in time and make quick decisions under special circumstances Adjustment.  
3. Formulate contingency plans and develop a crisis management team. In a special period like Covid -
19, the management team can introduce policies like purchase restrictions to ensure that demand 
shocks will not affect the market estimates of manufacturers an d suppliers. A bullwhip effect is less 
likely. 
 
Adaptability 
Adaptability is described as “the ability to adjust supply chain design to meet changes in market structure 
and to modify the supply network to reflect changes in strategy, technology and products. 
 
1. Directly assess the needs of end customers and direct customers. In this way, when the enterprises in 
the middle part of the supply chain only make production or supply decisions based on the demand 
information from their adjacent subordinate enterprises, the untruth of the demand information will go 
upstream along the supply chain, resulting in the phenomenon of gradual amplification. 
2. Determine the product's position in terms of technology and product life cycle. 
 
Alignment 
Alignment is described as the ability of a large company to "align the interests of all companies in its supply 
chain with its own". 
 
1. Clearly stipulate the roles and responsibilities of suppliers and customers, such as the purchase     
 
   
 
restriction policy. If in a special period, the behavior of customers hoarding goods and the loss of 
suppliers due to lack of goods have an impact on the manufacturer's assessment of the market, this can 
reduce the bullwhip effect. 
2. Free exchange of information with suppliers and customers, free exchange of information means better 
frequency of communication with the market, more communication can allow manufacturers to 
understand the impact of demand caused by special periods and allow manufacturers to better respond 
to Evaluate the current market demand and make changes. 
 
The portfolio approach 
The portfolio approach to supply chain architecture entails reducing supply chain risk by diversifying the 
portfolio of goods, suppliers, and distribution channels (Olavson et al., 2010). This method acknowledges 
that a range of events, including natural catastrophes, economic downturns, geopolitical events, and supplier 
failures, can cause supply chain interruptions, by disrupting transportation network, or cause damage to 
facilities or inventory. It's possible that a single supply chain design won't be str ong enough to withstand 
each danger. Consequently, by varying their supply chain designs, a portfolio strategy may assist businesses 
in risk management. 
By adopting a more thorough and proactive approach to risk management, the portfolio approach to supply 
chain risk management expands on conventional risk management approaches. This method involves 
prioritizing and managing risks using a combination of risk mitigation, risk transfer, and risk acceptance 
tactics after analysing hazards in terms of their potential impact and likelihood. The supply chain can be 
described as a portfolio of assets, with each investme nt representing a particular risk - this is the approach 
taken with the portfolio approach. While some dangers may have a significant impact and a high possibility, 
others may not. The supply chain management can gain a more in -depth view of the supply chain's total 
risk profile by evaluating each risk in this manner. 
The portfolio strategy, according to Olavson et al. (2010), entails creating a portfolio of supply chain 
architectures that differ in terms of their risk profile. This portfolio may contain many product categories, 
vendors, and routes of distribution, as w ell as various degrees of vertical integration. With riskier supply 
chain architectures offering higher potential rewards but also higher risk, the objective is to create a balance 
between risk and reward. reducing supply chain risk by diversifying the por tfolio of goods, suppliers, and 
distribution channels, acknowledges that a range of events, including natural catastrophes, economic 
downturns, geopolitical events, and supplier failures, can cause supply chain interruptions. It's possible that 
a single supply chain design won't be strong enough to withstand each danger. Consequently, by varying 
their supply chain designs, a portfolio strategy may assist businesses in risk management. After identifying 
and classifying the various portfolios and assets, organizations should assess the risks in terms of their 
likelihood and impact before prioritizing them using a combination of risk acceptance, transfer, and 
mitigation measures. 
 
The change in the supply chain of HP printers 
In the 1990s HP printer engines were manufactured in Asia where costs were low and then assembled and 
packaged into specific stock keeping units (SKUs) in a country closer to where demand was concentrated 
(Olavson et al., 2010). Producing printer engines abroad is an example of outsourcing and more specifically 
offshoring. HP deliberately postponed the packaging of engines into different SKUs until demand for the     
 
   
 
different SKUs was known (Olavson et al., 2010). This method is called postponement, which provided 
financial benefits for HP in the 1990s as it delivered customized products to customers at low costs. The 
unpredictable demand and high variety of HP printers shows it was an innovative product. The 
unpredictable demand caused HP to employ a responsive supply chain. The characteristics of responsive 
supply chains include high inventory and supplier choice based on speed, flexibility and quality. The supply 
chain of HP was optimized to meet consumer demand. 
 
Over the years the design of the HP supply chain has changed. The number of supply chains has increased, 
and postponement is less prominent. The location of manufacturing has also changed, and now  
manufacturing and assembly occur in the same country. The supply chain now consists of a responsive 
supply chain ( like that employed in the 1990s), a supply chain optimized for cost and a supply chain 
optimized for even lower costs (Olavson et al., 2010).  Multiple supply chains are needed to accommodate 
the different costs and delivery times for different products. The move away from postponement was caused 
by competitive price pressures which necessitated much lower costs than postponement provided (Olavson 
et al., 2010). Price pressures were also the motive behind the migration to countries where production and 
assembly could occur at an even lower cost. This shows how offshoring is now even more prominent for 
HP. 
 
Other market-driven factors caused changes in Hp’s supply chain. The printer market matured and so 
customer segments and market size were more defined and consequently fewer SKUs were needed 
(Olavson et al., 2010). These factors le d to postponement no longer being necessary . R esearch and 
development in the market also lead to improved product quality, consistency and longer life cycles. 
Consistent high-level production further reduces costs for repairs. All the price reductions contributed to 
price pressure which led to postponement becoming less economically viable for HP. Printers having 
reduced variety, more predictable demand, more consistent quality and a longer life cycle show how printers 
are becoming a more functional product.  They still exhibit Innovative characteristics however , e.g. high 
margins. The increased functional aspects of printers lead to supply chains being more efficient. Efficient 
supply chains exhibit low inventory and supplier choice is based on cost and quality. The supply chains are 
still a reflection of consumer demand as they were in the 1990s.  
Changes in the supply chain were also caused by changing financial goals. In the 1990s when printers were 
still in their infant stage, the emphasis was placed on increasing market share and revenue, so HP employed 
a responsive supply chain. As the market matured the priority switched to profitability , which led to 
offshoring to countries with even lower costs, reduced SKUs and the abandonment of postponement due to 
its lower profit margin (Olavson et al., 2010). However, postponement still exists in the high -end printer 
market, where market share is still the priority and variety is needed. This shows why a responsive supply 
chain is necessary, and why the number of HP supply chains has increased since the 1990s to fit responsive 
and less responsive supply chains.

MSCI151: Group Methex (Lent term)

• You will give a presentation during the week beginning March 6 , 202 3 (Week 1 8).  Your 
presentation slides should be uploaded to Moodle by 2:00pm on March 6, 2023. 
• Please name your presentation with your group name (e.g. “GroupC.pptx”, where C is your group

answer questions at the end of your presentation, which might last up to 5 minutes. 
• It is not necessary for all members of your group to speak during the presentation, but all members 
should attend and be prepared to answer questions. 
 
 
Part A 
 
A local grocery store sells two types of energy drinks: “Sprint” and “Vitality”.  The store has asked for your help 
to work out stock control policies for both drinks.  Daily demands for the drinks can be unpredictable, and the 
store wants to work out (i) when they should place orders for new stock, and (ii) how many units (bottles) of 
stock they should order at a time.  Their main objective is to minimise average daily inventory costs – taking into 
account holding costs, ordering costs and shortage costs for both products. 
 
The store has provided you with the following information about costs for the two drinks: 
 
 Sprint Vitality 
Holding cost per unit per day £0.05 £0.06 
Shortage cost per unit per day £1.20 £1.80 
Fixed ordering cost £30.00 £30.00 
Ordering cost per unit £0.60 £0.80 
 
The store’s inventory control policy works as follows: deliveries of new stock are received at the beginning of 
the day.  After receiving new stock, the store then incurs holding costs based on the current stock levels of both 
drinks.  During the day, demands are received for both drinks.  If the amount of demand for a drink on a particular 
day exceeds the stock level at the beginning of that day, then the store incurs shortage costs due to the loss of 
sales.  At the end of the day, the store inspects the stock levels for both drinks and decides whether or not to place 
orders for new stock.  They wish to use the following type of system: 
 
• If the current stock level for Sprint, plus the number of units of Sprint that they have ordered but are still 
awaiting delivery of, is less than or equal to a certain fixed number (call this 𝐿𝑆), they will place an order 
for a certain fixed number of units of Sprint (call this 𝑄𝑆). 
• If the current stock level for Vitality, plus the number of units of Vitality that they have ordered but are 
still awaiting delivery of, is less than or equal to a certain fixed number (call this 𝐿𝑉), they will place an 
order for a certain fixed number of units of Vitality (call this 𝑄𝑉). 
   2 
The numbers 𝐿𝑆 and 𝐿𝑉 are known as “re -order levels”, and the numbers 𝑄𝑆 and 𝑄𝑉 are known as “order 
quantities”.  Note that on a particular day the store may decide to place orders for both drinks, or only one type 
of drink (e.g. Sprint only), or neither of the drinks. 
 
The two drinks are ordered from different suppliers – call these Supplier A (for Sprint) and Supplier B (for 
Vitality).  The lead time for Supplier A is expected to be 4 days.  This means that when an order is placed, it will 
usually arrive 4 days later.  However, based on past experience, the store believes there is a 10% chance that 
Supplier A will deliver one day late (i.e. after 5 days).  For Supplier B, the lead time is expected to be 3 days, but 
there is a 15% chance that they will deliver one day late (i.e. after 4 days).  If an order is placed at the end of Day 
𝑛, then it will be received at the beginning of Day  𝑛 + 𝑡 + 1, where 𝑡 is the lead time.  For example, if an order 
is placed at the end of Day 10 and the lead time is 4 days, it will be received at the beginning of Day 15. 
 
As an example (to show how the process works in more detail), suppose that at the beginning of a particular day, 
the store has 50 bottles of Sprint in stock, and they are also waiting for 70 bottles to be delivered – but these have 
not yet arrived.  Also suppose they are using a re-order level 𝐿𝑆 = 100 and an order quantity 𝑄𝑆 = 70.  Then: 
• The holding costs incurred are £(50 × 0.05) = £2.50. 
• The shortage costs depend on the daily demand.  If the daily demand is 50 or less, there will be no 
shortage (the store can satisfy all of the demand).  But if the demand is 60 (for example), then there will 
be a shortage of (60 − 50) = 10, so the shortage cost will be £(10 × 1.20) = £12. 
• Whether or not the store places an order at the end of the day also depends on the demand.  They are 
already waiting for an order of 70 units to be delivered, so if the stock level at the end of the day is more 
than 30 (i.e. if the daily demand is less than 20), then their stock level (including units being delivered) 
will be more than 100, which is the value of 𝐿𝑆.  So in that case they will not place an order.  But if the 
daily demand is 30 (for example), then the stock level (including units being delivered) will be 20 +
70 = 90, and this is smaller than 𝐿𝑆, so they will place an order for 𝑄𝑆 = 70 units to be delivered.  The 
cost of this order is given by adding the fixed order cost to the number of units ordered times the ordering 
cost per unit, so it will be £(30 + 70 × 0.60) = £72. 
 
The total inventory costs for the day are given by adding up the holding costs, shortage costs and ordering costs 
described above.  This must be done for both drinks. 
 
To help you understand the demand patterns for the two drinks, the store has provided you with a dataset showing 
a history of daily demands for the two drinks over a period of one year (365 days).  In some cases these demands 
have been estimated, because they do not know exactly how many bottles they would have sold on days when 
they were unable to satisfy all demand.  See the file demand_history.xlsx for the demand history.   As 
you can see, t he demands vary significantly from day to day, so you should try to find suitable random 
distributions to model the variations in demand for both drinks. 
 
The store has asked you to help them set the re -order levels (𝑳𝑺 and 𝑳𝑽) and the order quantities (𝑸𝑺 and 
𝑸𝑽) in order to minimise their average daily costs.   In order to do this, you should set up a simulation model 
(using Excel or other software of your choice) and experiment with changing the values of  𝐿𝑆, 𝐿𝑉, 𝑄𝑆 and 𝑄𝑉 in 
order to find the values that give the smallest possible average daily costs. 
 
Can you find the optimal values of 𝐿𝑆, 𝐿𝑉, 𝑄𝑆 and 𝑄𝑉, and what is the average daily cost if your recommended 
values are used?

Part B 
 
The store would also like you to investigate another question.  They have the option of ordering the “Sprint” 
drink from a different supplier – call this Supplier C.  Supplier C offers to deliver orders more quickly than 
Supplier A, so if Supplier C is used, the lead time will usually be only 2 days, but there is also a 10% chance that 
the lead time will be 3 days.  However, Supplier C charges a fixed ordering cost of £40, so it is more expensive 
to place an order with Supplier C compared to Supplier A.  The store wants you to investigate whether they 
should order Sprint from Supplier A or Supplier C.  (Note that if Supplier C is used, the values of 𝐿𝑆 and 𝑄𝑆 
could be different from the values used for Supplier A.  In other words, the store is able to make adjustments to 
the re-order level and order quantity depending on which supplier is used.) 
 
Do you recommend that the store should order Sprint from Supplier C, or should they continue to use Supplier 
A?  If Supplier C is used, what should the re-order level and order quantity be? 
 
 
Part C 
 
Now suppose that Suppliers A and B have merged together, so that there is now a single supplier that is able to 
supply both drinks (forget about Supplier C in this part).  This means that the store can save money on the fixed 
ordering costs by placing orders for both drinks at the same time.  This works as follows: if the store places orders 
for both Sprint and Vitality on the same day, then they only need to pay the fixed ordering cost of £30 once.  For 
example, if they order 70 units of Sprint and 80 unit s of Vitality on the same day, the total cost of the order will 
be £(30 + 70 × 0.60 + 80 × 0.80) = £136.  If they place an order for only one of the drinks on a particular day, 
the fixed ordering cost will still be the same as before, i.e. £30. 
 
In this part you may assume that if an order is placed (whether it’s for both drinks or only one of the drinks), the 
lead time will usually be 4 days but there is a 10% chance that it will be 5 days. 
 
Given this new situation, the store would like to ask you what their ordering policy should be in order to take 
advantage of the possibility of saving money by placing orders for both drinks at the same time.  In this part, you 
can experiment with different types of ordering systems that work differently from the ones in Part A and Part B.  
For example, you might try using a rule where the re-order level for one drink on a particular day becomes smaller 
if an order for the other drink has already been placed on the same day (to make it more likely that the store will 
place orders for both drinks at the same time). 
 
What should the store’s ordering policy be in order to minimise average daily costs?

1. First Task Overview (Alpha Blend) 
 
Fastronomic already had a model to determine the blend of powders 
for their Alpha product, which was created and calculated using Excel. Their 
first request was to convert this model to Python , which is a powerful  and 
robust programming language  that allows for more technical flexibility, as 
well as the ability to create a user -friendly interface, which isn’t possible on 
Excel. Because of this, and the global issue of ‘big data’ and the increasing 
demand for its’ analysis  in business, Python is becomin g widely adopted in 
many industries.  
The conversion was relatively simple, and for the analysis a tool called 
‘PuLP’ was used. This  is an online library or ‘plug-in’ used to solve linear 
programming problems on Python. The results from this model aligned with 
Fastronomic’s model, which verified that everything was accurate and 
working. The resulting proportions of ingredient  powders (base, protein, 
carbohydrates, and oil) for the Alpha blend from the Python model were very 
similar to the results from their  Excel model, with some very minor 
differences in the decimal points. I have been informed that these differences 
are expected and  are within allowable tolerances , so are not a cause for 
concern.  
 
1.1- Methodology 
The first step in the process was to set up the linear programming (LP) 
problem. Most LPs are laid out in a similar template- create the mode, define 
the variables, set an objective function, add constraints, then solve and print. 
The objective function is what tells the program whether you want to 
maximise or minimise something when optimising.  
In the case of Fastronomic Alpha, their objective is to minimise the total 
cost of the ingredients used per 125g portion. This is defined as the sum of 
the cost /gram of each  individual ingredient * amount (in grams) of each 
ingredient used. 
Next, we define the constraints for the problem. These constraints 
represent the nutritional requirements for the product, which include energy,  Fastronomic ‘Alpha’ vs ‘Omega’- product and Supply Chain Analysis and Optimisation 
fat, carbohydrate, protein, salt, and fibre. Each of these requirements was 
expressed as a linear inequality, with the total nutritional contribution from all 
ingredients being as close to the  recommended daily amount. Additionally, 
the total weight of all ingredients used must equal the portion size of 125g.  
Non-negativity constraints were also included, meaning t hat the 
amount of each ingredient used cannot be less than zero - which does 
actually happen in another model , discussed later . After defining the 
problem, we used the solve() function from the PuLP library to find the 
optimal solution. 
 
1.2- Results and Evaluation 
The solution provided by the solver included the optimal amounts of 
each ingredient to use in the Fastronomic Alpha product, as well as the total 
cost per portion. These results were found to be in close agreement with the 
amounts provided by the company, with minor discrepancies likely due to 
differences in rounding and numerical precision between Excel and Pytho n:

Executive Summary 
This report has been conducted to analyse the performance of a Bike -Share Rental 
Company in Seoul, spanning the period of December 2017 -November 2018. The 
company provides a service for customers to rent and share a bike they can use to 
cycle around the city. 
This company has provided data on the daily number of rentals, in addition to a range 
of weather data per day . The provided data has shown that there is a very clear 
cyclical trend of popularity of bike rentals, with significantly fewer bike rentals 
during certain seasons compared to others. The weather data has also shown that the 
weather does have a noticeable impact on bike rental rates in Seoul. 
 
Some limitations arose during the analysis. Many of the weather variables may have 
intervened with the analysis, as there were many codependent/interdependent 
variables. Perhaps they could consider measuring fewer, but more relevant variables- 
for example visibility and humidity (which didn’t seem to have much effect) could 
be replaced with simply measuring temperature and rain. 
Another recommendation would be to include data more relevant to the operation 
and management of the business. The weather is not something the company can 
adjust or change, so there is a limitation to t he usefulness of the statistics. One 
recommendation would be to i nclude a variety of information other than weather - 
such as internal business factors such as profit and loss, as this would provide the 
company with metrics they can actively change and work on, so that they can satisfy 
their objectives. Additionally, external factors such as tourism rates, can also be an 
important one to consider.

1. Introduction 
 
1.1 Background on the Study and the Company 
All companies should consider if they have any seasonal trend in popularity, as this 
can help them adjust their objectives during the year. Seasonality may affect different 
companies differently, and some may not have any. This can be dependent on the 
nature of a business, or naturally cyclical events such as weather. 
Seoul is a city with a temperate climate with four distinct seasons - spring, summer, 
autumn, winter. Seoul’s climate means that the differences between summer and 
winter can be very extreme. A s a result, this can have a heavy impact on services 
such as bike rental companies, where customers and tourists rely on weather when 
they decide on their daily activities. Therefore, it is especially for the company to 
consider this. 
 
1.2 Aims of the Analysis and its’ Potential Influence 
The aim of this report is to show how significant the impact of different variables, 
such as wind, rain, and solar radiation is, on the amount of interested cyclists. The 
data provided by the company has been used to visualise seasonal trends, as well as 
identify the impact of different weather variables on bike rental rates . Using this 
analysis, the company can determine timings of certain business decisions such as 
staffing or inventory, to more efficiently allocate resources. Additionally, this report 
can show how efficiently they are already operating. 
 
1.3.1 Methodology 
The analysis was done using analytical and graphical linear regression. Regression 
data, specifically R numbers and P numbers were ident ified, and were used to 
consider whether certain variables were significant or not. Multiple linear regression 
involved grouping all (or some) of the variables, to see the significance of the data 
sets as a whole. Graphical analysis showed the regression data visually, so that it can 
be understood more quickly and clearly. 
Seasonal trends were identified using trendlines with varying moving average 
periods, to smooth out irregularities and anomalies. These anomalies were caused 
by irregular weather, as well as the fact that there were 13 non-operational days out 
of the 366 days. This is shown in Figure 1, where the red trendline has a 34-period 
moving average. This was sufficient to show a clear trend, without compromising 
too much of the data.  
 
1.3.1 Methodology Evaluation  MSCI152- Report on Bike-Share Rental Company 4 
Since there was data for every day over the course of a year, there was a sufficient 
sample size to conduct accurate multiple linear regres sion. However,  not all 
regression models were appropriate, and some violated some assumptions for 
regression modelling. Some variables had multicollinearity, which meant the effect 
of individual variables on the companies’ performance could not be clearly separated. 
This may have artificially inflated the statistical significance of certain variables. As 
a result, not all variables were considered equally.  
Further evaluation on the appropriateness of the data and regression models will be 
discussed later in the regression analysis section of this report (sections 2.x). 
 
 
1.4 Findings- Seasonality 
The findings show there is a clear seasonal trend, with less bike rentals during winter 
and spring months, and a steep increase from summer through autumn. This is likely 
to be due to less bicycle-friendly conditions due to rain, wind and/or snow in certain 
times of the year, and dry, sunny weather bringing in more outdoor enthusiasts. 
(More in-depth analysis of the impact of certain weather variables will be included 
later in this report, in the regression analysis section s 2.x).  
The peak happens to be during summer holiday season around July/August 2018 (as 
shown in Figure 1), which could be caused for example by a surge of tourism into 
Seoul; however, data on tourism was not provided.

2.1.1 R Squared Value- Evaluation 
Firstly, the R Square value given is 0.66. this means that the model including all the 
weather data accounts for about 66% of the bike rental data, or that the correlation 
value is 66%. This shows that there is a noticeable correlation between t he weather 
data and bike rentals, although it is not very strong. About 34% of the bike rental 
data must be explained by other factors. This must mean that either there are factors 
that have not been measured, or that some of the existing factors may be insignificant 
enough to be ruining this model. 
 
2.1.2 F value- Evaluation 
The significance F value in this case is practically 0.00. This highlights that there is 
in fact a statistically significant correlation in this model, and the results may not 
have occurred by chance. 
 
2.1.3 Coefficient- Evaluation 
The coefficient is one way of seeing how significantly a variable affects the bike 
rental rates. Some variables have negative or positive coefficients. For example, if 
average dew point temperature were to go up by one unit one day, it is predicted that 
bike rental rates would be about 479.4 higher that day since it has a positive 
coefficient. On the other hand, if rain was to be increased by one unit, this would 
decrease the bike rental rates by 28.27. Averag e visibility has a coefficient close to 
0, which would mean a relatively big change in visibility wouldn’t have a very 
significant impact on bike rentals. As a result, this variable may be ignored, to create 
a more accurate regression model. 
However, this poses an issue - some variables have extremely sensitive/insensitive 
units. In the data set provided, a verage visibility values range from 214.29 to 2000, 
which is a very broad range of values, whereas solar radiation ranges from 0 to 1.22. 
in practice, the difference between and 1.22MJ/m2 of solar radiation is night and day, 
whereas the difference between 200 and 201.22 visibility is unnoticeable. Because 
of this, either the units must be adjusted, or these variables must be ignored to 
improve the accuracy of the coefficient of this model.  
 
2.1.4 P value- Evaluation 
P value is another statistical test to see how significant a variable is. In this model 
the only statistically significant variables, with a P value under 0.01 (which is 
generally considered goo d), are wind, solar radiation, and rain. This questions the 
appropriateness of this model, as this means that most of the other variables should 
be ignored from this model, as it means that it must violate some assumptions for 
regression modelling.  MSCI152- Report on Bike-Share Rental Company 7 
One of the assumptions this violates is multicollinearity. Logically, a variable like 
temperature, which has a very high P value, will have a strong correlation with others 
such as snow, or dew point temperature. This means that the effect of the individual 
variables cannot be clearly separated, so the regression equation becomes unstable.  
Another assumption broken is homoscedasticity. Simple linear regression graphing 
(figure 3, figure 4 ) shows that some variables such as dew point don’t follow

Q1 
 
The objective is to determine the optimal combination of volumes of feedstocks and 
alcohols, to produce the required volumes of gasoline at the lowest cost. Pacific 
Refinery Company (PR co) produces regular, high -test and premium gasoline, by 
blending varying amounts of 89-octane and 95 -octane feedstocks, with varying 
amounts of ethyl and methyl alcohols. Each type of gasoline  produced must adhere 
to specified octane  rating requirements and production targets, and there are 
specified amounts of feedstock and alcohols available.  
 
 
Variables 
 
Each variable represents the separate volumes (in gallons) of each type of feedstock 
(89-octane = F89x, 95-octane = F95x) and alcohol (Ethyl = Ex, Methyl = Mx) added to 
each type of gasoline blend (Regular = X R, High-test = X H, Premium = X P).  Note- 
Premium gasoline may only contain Ethyl alcohol, therefore there is no variable ‘MP’: 
 
- F89R; gallons of 89-octane Feedstock added to Regular gasoline 
- F89H; gallons of 89-octane Feedstock added to High-test gasoline 
- F89P; gallons of 89-octane Feedstock added to Premium gasoline 
- F95R; gallons of 95-octane Feedstock added to Regular gasoline 
- F95H; gallons of 95-octane Feedstock added to High-test gasoline 
- F95P; gallons of 95-octane Feedstock added to Premium gasoline 
- ER; gallons of Ethyl alcohol added to Regular gasoline 
- EH; gallons of Ethyl alcohol added to High-test gasoline 
- EP; gallons of Ethyl alcohol added to Premium gasoline 
- MR; gallons of Methyl alcohol added to Regular gasoline 
- MH; gallons of Methyl alcohol added to High-test gasoline 
 
The following variables can be added together to calculate the total volumes of each 
ingredient used, and gasoline produced: 
 
- F89R + F89H + F89P = total volume of 89-octane Feedstock used 
- F95R + F95H + F95P = total volume of 95-octane Feedstock used 
- ER + EH + EP = total volume of Ethyl alcohol used 
- MR + MH + MP = total volume of Methyl alcohol used 
 
- F89R + F95R + ER + MR = total volume of Regular gasoline produced 
- F89H + F95H + EH + MH = total volume of High-test gasoline produced 
- F89P + F95P + EP = total volume of Premium gasoline produced 
 
 
Objective function 
 
The objective is to minimise the total production cost  (C). This cost is calculated 
based on the total volumes of each ingredient used in gallons, multiplied by their 
respective prices per gallon (in £s). The objective function to be minimised is: 
   
 
C = 1.00 × (F89R + F89H + F89P) + 1.50 × (F95R + F95H + F95P) + 1.25 × (ER + EH + 
EP) + 0.80 × (MR + MH) 
 
 
Constraints 
 
The constraints represent the limitations, specifications and requirements of the 
variables in the problem. 
 
 
Ingredient availability- There are limited amounts of feedstock and alcohols available 
(in gallons) , so the  following variable totals cannot exceed these amounts . These 
constraints represent the upper bound of these variables’ domains: 
 
- F89R + F89H + F89P <= 18,000 (89-octane Feedstock availability) 
- F95R + F95H + F95P <= 15,000 (95-octane Feedstock availability) 
- ER + EH + EP <= 4000 (Ethyl alcohol availability) 
- MR + MH <= 5210 (Methyl alcohol availability) 
 
 
Production requirements- These are the required amounts of each type of gasoline 
which must be produced (in gallons), which means the totals of these variables must 
assumably be exactly equal to these amounts: 
 
- F89R + F95R + ER + MR = 15,000 (Regular gasoline) 
- F89H + F95= + EH + MH = 12,000 (High-test gasoline) 
- F89P + F95P + EP = 6780 (Premium gasoline) 
 
 
Alcohol volume limits - These constraints limit the amount s of alcohols contained in 
the gasoline to specified percentages. Regular gasoline can contain up to 5% total 
alcohols; high-test up to 10% total alcohols; premium can only contain ethyl alcohol 
up to 5% . These constraints work because if the amounts of alcohol(s), E + M, is 
greater than the specified percentage of the total gasoline volume, x% * (F89 + F95 
+ E + M), the left-hand-side would be positive, violating the constraint: 
 
- ER + MR - (0.05 * (F89R + F95R + ER + MR)) <= 0 (Alcohols in Regular 
gasoline) 
EH + MH - (0.10 * (F89H + F95H + EH + MH)) <= 0 (alcohols in High-test 
gasoline) 
- EP - (0.05 * (F89P + F95P + EP)) <= 0 (Ethyl alcohol in Premium gasoline) 
 
 
Octane rating requirements - The average octane rating s for each type of gasoline 
must be at least 91 for regular gasoline, at least 93 for high -test, and at least 95 for 
premium. O ctane ratings are calculated as the average octane ratings for the 
ingredients, weighted by volume . These constraints ensure that the total octane 
contribution from each ingredient, 89*F89 + 95*F95 + 120*E + 110*M , is more than 
or equal to the total required octane , x * F89 + F95 + E + M , otherwise the right -
hand-side would be less than 0:   
 
 
- (89*F89R + 95*F95R + 120*ER + 110*MR) - (91 * (F89R + F95R + ER + MR)) >= 
0 (Regular gasoline) 
- (89*F89H + 95*F95H + 120*EH + 110*MH) - (93 * (F89H + F95H + EH + MH)) >= 
0 (High-test gasoline) 
- (89*F89P + 95*F95P + 120*EP) - (95 * (F89P + F95P + EP)) >= 0 (Premium 
gasoline) 
 
 
Non-negativity constraints - These make sure that none of the variable values fall 
below 0 to ensure a feasible, realistic solution . They also represent the lower bound 
of the variable domains: 
 
- F89R >= 0 
- F89H >= 0 
- F89P >= 0 
- F95R >= 0 
- F95H >= 0 
- F95P >= 0 
- ER >= 0 
- EH >= 0 
- EP >= 0 
- MR >= 0 
- MH >= 0

function per unit increase in the right -hand-side of the constraint. Therefore, row 6 of 
this dual price column should provide the same results as the change in total 
production cost column (divided by 1000, as this column shows the change per 1000   
 
change in the right -hand-side of the constraint, rather than per unit change) - and it 
does, as they are essentially showing the same thing on a different scale. 
 
The results show that the linearity of the relationship between total cost and amount 
of regular gasoline needed, ( /the gradient of the graph, or the ‘constantness’ of the 
dual price), seem to change at two points - around 12 -13,000 gallons, and around 
8000-9000 gallons. Using a potentially tedious, manual process of adjusting the RHS 
of the constraint at around these points  (playing ‘higher or lower’ until the dual price 
value changes, e.g. 12,000, then 13,000, then 12,500, then 12,250 etc)  and 
checking the output, will allow to pinpoint at which exact point the dual price value 
changes, and therefore provide a more accurate representation of the relationship 
between cost and amount of gasoline required.  
 
Using this method s hows that at F89R + F95 R + ER + M R = 12111 the dual price is 
still at -1.465000- however changes to -1.251250 at 12110. 
 
Again, F89R + F95R + ER + MR = 8672, the dual price is at -1.251250, and changes 
to -1.050000 at 8671. 
 
 
Implications 
 
This means that if the requirement for regular gasoline was to decrease from 15,000 
by 2889 gallons, the decrease in total cost will be linear at £1.465 per gallon 
decreased. After this point, a further decrease in the requirement for regular gasoline 
from 12,110 to 8672 gallons, will result in a linear decrease in cost of £1.25125 per 
gallon. A decrease from 8671 to 0 gallons required, will result in a £1.05** decrease 
in total cost, per gallon.  
 
This proves that the relationship is in a way  linear, but with 2 ‘kinks’ in linearity  at 
8672 and 12,111 gallons of required regular gasoline - the relationship is linear 
between 0 - 8671 gallons with a ‘gradient’ of 1.05; linear between 8672 - 12,110 
gallons with a ‘gradient’ of 1.25125; and linear between 12,111 -15,000+ gallons with 
a ‘gradient’ of 1.465. 
 
Q4 
i) 
 
 
To ensure that PR uses at least twice as much Ethyl alcohol as Methyl alcohol, a 
new constraint must be added that represents this. The original LP formulation can 
stay the same (converted to standard form) , with the exact same objective function, 
variables and constraints- the additional constraint to be implemented is:  
 
ER + EH + EP - 2 * (MR + MH) >= 0 
 
ER + E H + E P represents the total volume of Ethyl alcohol used throughout all the 
gasoline types, and MR + MH represents the total volume of Methyl alcohol used. This   
 
constraint ensures that the total Ethy l is equal to or greater than two times the total 
Methyl, otherwise the right-hand-side would be less than 0. 
 
Converting into standard form so that it is an equality (and that the RHS is non -
negative which it already is, as 0 is sufficient): 
 
ER + EH + EP - 2 * (MR + MH) + Sx = 0 
 
(All other constraints converted to standard form should also contain slack variables 
S2, S3 etc- in Sx case, x may vary depending on the order of the constraints - e.g. if 
this is the first constraint  in the LP , it would be S 1 so that each constraint has a 
separate slack variable.) 
 
 
ii) 
 
A new variable must be introduced, Y, that represents the shortfall, in gallons, of 
high-test gasoline production - this variable will be added to the production 
requirements constraint for high-test gasoline: 
 
F89H + F95H + EH + MH + Y = 12000 
 
This will mean that Y = the shortfall between what is required, minus how much 
would be produced- rearranging the equation, means that: 
 
Y = 12000 – (F89H + F95H + EH + MH) 
 
 
Converting the constraint to standard form by adding a slack variable: 
 
F89H + F95H + EH + MH + Y + Sx = 12000 
 
(All other constraints converted to standard form should also contain slack variables 
S2, S3 etc- in Sx case, x may vary depending on the order of the constraints - e.g. if 
this is the first constraint  in the LP , it would be S 1 so that each constraint has a 
separate slack variable.) 
 
 
Additionally, this constraint must be added to the objective function, as it is another 
variable that contributes to the total cost, with a ‘price’/coefficient of £2 per gallon: 
 
C = 1.00 × (F89R + F89H + F89P) + 1.50 × (F95R + F95H + F95P) + 1.25 × (ER + EH + 
EP) + 0.80 × (MR + MH) + 2 * Y 
 
 
Lastly, this new variable must also be non-negative: 
 
Y >= 0

 Congress Office Chair Plant – System Description 
Congress is a company that manufactures office furniture. One site is dedicated to a particular office 
chair. The plant takes a fabric sheet, a set of bars for the frame and a pre-made foam cushion and 
assembles these into the office chair. The chairs are also stored in a small warehouse onsite (total 
capacity is 100 chairs). This warehouse also acts as a distribution centre – as orders come in, they are 
processed before the correct number of chairs are collected ready to be shipped to the purchaser. 
Operations take place between 9am and 5pm, seven days a week. All staff take a break between 
12:30pm and 1pm for lunch. You may assume that any processes still going on at 12:30pm or 5pm 
are left as they are and picked up again when the shift continues. 
Fabric Sheet Delivery and Processing 
The fabric sheets are delivered every two days, at 8am, with a delivery of 150 sheets. The capacity of 
the inventory for fabric sheets is 500. If the delivery of 150 sheets takes the capacity beyond 500, the 
remaining are returned at no cost. 
The fabric sheet first needs to be cut to the correct size and shape. This is done using one of two 
cutting machines. An upholsterer (a fabric worker within the factory) first loads the sheet into the 
machine. The cutting process is then automated and takes exactly 7 minutes. The upholsterer is then 
needed to unload the cut sheet and take it to a set of shelves (which only has space for 10 pieces of 
fabric). It waits there until an upholsterer is ready to do the sewing work to make the chair cover. 
This can be at one of three sewing machines. Note that there are currently only three upholsterers 
working on the site. After this, they are placed in a buffer with space for 50 covers to await the final 
assembly. 
Frame kit Delivery and Processing 
A delivery of 100 sets of metal frame bars occurs everyday at 10am. The storage for these sets can 
hold 500. As with the fabric sheets, if the delivery takes the capacity beyond 500, the remaining are 
returned at no cost. 
The sets must first be welded together. There are three welding stations, and the full process takes 
on average 15 minutes. After this they are placed in a buffer that can store 15 completed frames, 
ready for assembly. 
Cushion Delivery 
The cushions themselves are delivered in the state needed for the chair, so do not undergo any 
further processing before the full chair is assembled. 
The inventory storage space has enough capacity for 600 cushions. They are delivered every 2 days 
at 3pm, and 150 are delivered. As with the fabric sheets and metal frame bars, if the delivery takes 
the capacity beyond 600, the remaining are returned at no cost. 
Assembly and Warehouse 
The assembly is performed by 5 members of staff at 5 assembly stations. It is a long process, 
requiring the cushions to be secured into the frames and the covers stapled on. The completed 
chairs are then stored in the warehouse. 
The warehouse is split into two sections, one for small orders and one for large orders. Both sections 
have capacity for 50 chairs. The allocation of a chair to a section is based on which has the most free 
space.  Orders and Order Processing 
There are two types of order: small (which consist of a single chair) and large (which consist of 20 
chairs).  These can happen at any time of day, as they are made through an online system. Each 
order must first be processed by a receptionist. They are then added to the list of orders that must 
be collected together before being shipped. Two separate queues are used here, one for small 
orders and one for large orders. One worker is assigned to each queue, and it takes a little time to 
get the chairs from the warehouse, and this can only be done if the chairs are available. Once the full 
quota of chairs for the order are collected, the order is shipped. At this point, the order is considered 
complete. The aim of Congress is to complete 95% of orders within 24 hours of it being placed. 
Data 
The available data include the following: 
• 200 chairs were monitored through all the stages of their production. The durations (in 
minutes) of each process in the manufacturing were monitored and collected; 
• The number of large and small orders over a 13-week period; 
• For the orders in the last two weeks of that period, the time it took to process the order and 
the time it took to collect the chairs together were collected (both in minutes). 
• A collection of 40 weeks from last year were monitored from a performance perspective. For 
each week, the average time it took to process orders (small and large separately, both in 
minutes) and the total number of orders completed was noted. 
Overall Task 
The company has approached you to model their operations using simulation. They are particularly 
interested in the delivery policy, as they feel fewer deliveries may be possible to reduce costs. 
However, there is concern that if this was done, there may be times when the stock runs short, 
leading to orders not being processed within 24 hours. There are also questions related to whether a 
quality control procedure should be implemented within the plant. 
See the next page for the specific tasks. 
Hint 
You may find pages 91 and 92 of the Witness reference manual useful for more complex input and 
output rules. 
   Question 1: Conceptual Model [25 marks] 
Provide a full conceptual model for your simulation model of the plant and its operations, providing 
all the necessary details. Following this, state any distributions used with a justification for their 
selection. 
Question 2: Validation [15 marks] 
Give full details of any validation procedures you used for this model.  
Question 3: Inventory Control Deliveries [25 marks] 
One of the key questions the company is asking is whether an alternative delivery schedule could be 
applied for fabric, frame kits and cushions. Each delivery has a fixed charge, regardless of how many 
items are delivered, so reducing the number of deliveries would reduce the overall cost. The time 
between deliveries must be a whole number of days and the quantity being delivered must be a 
multiple of 50. 
Come up with alternative plan to improve the costs and evaluate it, providing confidence and 
prediction intervals for each of the following key performance measures: 
a) Mean time between an order being placed and the items being shipped (for both small and 
large orders); and 
b) The percentage of orders shipped within 24 hours of being placed. 
Compare your proposed plan with the current plan based on the same measures. Are the differences 
statistically significant? 
Question 4: Analysis of Bottlenecks and Potential Improvements [15 marks] 
The company are interested in identifying any bottlenecks that could help the system function more 
smoothly. Identify one such point (including some evidence for this) and suggest an improvement 
that could be made. Improvements could be one of the following: 
• Adding an additional machine or workstation; 
• Adding one additional member of staff; 
• Increasing the size of one storage/buffer space;

Introduction- Inditex vs. Shein 
Just before the pandemic, Inditex- the parent company of household fashion names such 
as Zara and Bershka - had the second strongest supply chain in the world, according to 
Gartner’s Supply Chain Top 25 ranking of 2019. As a mere fashion company, it s’ supply 
chain dominated against some of the highest-grossing companies in the world from even 
bigger industries, such as Nestle, Intel and Walmart1.  
Over the next consecutive years, it fell to ninth place2, then 13 th 3, then 18 th 4. In 2023, it 
managed to recover back to 13th place5. Of course, the Gartner Top 25 ranking is not a 
perfect measure as supply chains are incredibly complex mechanisms, and it is arguably 
inappropriate to compare one companies’ supply chain against another’s. However,  this 
data goes to show the mid /long-term impact that the pandemic had on Inditex’s supply 
chain robustness.  
One company that has never been named on this list is Shein, and due to its’ controversial 
practices, it is unlikely to ever be named a top 25 supply chai n. Shein is known for their 
suspiciously cheaply priced clothing, as well as their numerous lawsuits and investigations 
against them, such as racketeering, tax law abuses, and allegations of forced labour 6. 
Despite this, (or arguably because of this,) the mysterious online fast fashion brand  has 
seen an exponential rise, very much thanks to the pandemic. The company was founded 
in 2008 as ZZKKO, which is almost surprising to some, as it only began to gather any sort 
of attention  around 2016, 
according to Google Trends  
(figure 1) . They didn’t need to 
stabilize their supply chain after 
this external shock, which was 
catastrophic to most of the 
economy- on the contrary- they 
thrived and became wh at they 
are now because of it. 
Zara, Bershka and most other retailers who rely heavily (or completely) on brick -and-
mortar stores, suffered heavy losses in sales and demand, due to global quarantines and 
supply chain shocks. Customers could no longer purchase products in shops, shipments 
were cancelled, and the flow of raw materials and finished goods was disrupted , which 
additionally resulted in disruptions at the manufacturing end of the supply chain - like a 
bullwhip effect on a massive scale, and with fluctuations at both ends of the metaphorical 
whip. Inditex managed to stabilize relatively quickly and efficiently, by adjusting their 
supply chain and business model to cater to online shoppers. However countless retailers 
that couldn’t adapt in time were forced  to lay off staff, close stores, or even file for 
bankruptcy. This list contains former high-street giants such as Debenhams, Topshop and 
JCPenney7.  
Meanwhile, a revolution was beginning in the fashion industry among companies whose 
supply chains were better suited to this shock, mainly by being able to switch to (or already 
being based) online. This sort of direct -to-customer business model was becoming a

necessity, and some companies were better or worse equipped to deal with the 
unprecedented need to cut out of the ‘middleman’ in the form of physical shops. Not only 
was this extra step in the supply chain suddenly shut off, but some companies realized it 
was just an unnecessary cost money wise, as well as time wise. Shein realized this quickly 
and used the coronavirus pandemic as a trampoline to build a global, online fashion giant 
that can produce hundreds of thousands of new products a week, and still manage to get 
these products delivered from one end of the supply chain straight to the customers front 
door within a  couple of weeks - a process  that usually takes other companies  several  
months.
