Traditionally in fast fashion  supply chain 
strategy, according to ( Tokatli, 2008) 11, 
there are five requirements.  One of the

rooms, as well as the introduction of their new Zara Beauty range with fragrances that you

Zara had 2,312 stores globally as of 2022, however this number has decreased yearly

a combination of the need to  mitigate costs by temporarily shutting down stores , as well 
as a strategic decision to adapt to the increasing shift in consumer behaviour towards

significant supply chain challenge that Inditex handled well, thanks to their already diverse 
multi-channel selling of merchandise. Zara already had a significant online presence 
before the pandemic unlike many traditional fashion brands , therefore overall loss in 
performance was mitigated as they had other successful channels they could rely on other 
than physical shops.  
It may seem that this is an Achilles’ Heel for Shein, being online-only. However, they have 
also taken advantage of multi -channel selling, with temporary pop -up ‘tours’ across 
Europe14, starting as soon as covid restrictions began getting lifted. These ‘concert -tour’-

aware of the power of bricks and mortar, and allows them to harness this power for an 
extra performance boost without having to invest additionally into permanent retail stores.

Zara and Shein have both mastered efficient production timelines, with ‘super-responsive’ 
and ‘rapid-fire’ supply chains, that ‘make certain that deliveries are sufficiently frequent’ -
which happens to be Tokatli’s fourth requirement in fast fashion. Zara, just like the rest of 
the economy, though, were unavoidably disrupted during the pandemic  by delayed 
shipments and cancellations , causing their deliveries to not be as frequent as usual. 
Regardless of this , one  of the bottlenecks of any fast fashion brand’ s supply chain is 
predicting design trends, communicating this information to designers and production staff, 
and then getting the items manufactured and shipped, in order to get the most fashionable 
clothing in to the customers hands before they become outdated . This necessity to 
‘connect customers' demand with the upstream operations of design, procurement, 
production, and distribution ,’ is Tokatli’s second requirement.  Shein had pioneered a 
solution to this problem by developing an information algorithm , utilising artificial 
intelligence to identify popular designs automatically, and get ting them communicated to 
producers as quickly as possible. This allows their supply strategy to be even more pull 
based, and allows faster responsiveness to customer demand. Unfortunately, this solution 
had backfired for them, as these algorithms sometimes resulted in direct plagiarism, which 
caused an addition to their list of legal troubles. This highlights a potential trade -off 
between efficiency and ethical considerations in their supply chain management. 
It is highly likely this solution was made possible indirectly by the pandemic. Despite the 
economic slowdown in other sectors, the AI industry saw strong growth in 2020, thanks to 
a growth of total global investment in AI of 40% from 2019 -2020, compared to only 12% 
from 2018 -201915. Most industries were forced to invest more into their information 
technology to adjust to the shift to online, and artificial intelligence at the time was an 
emergingly promising IT tool. This suggests interdependence between industries and how 
even a  global crisis often has its silver linings - Shein took advantage of an emerging 
technology in an unconventional way to improve their supply chain.  
 
‘Third, fast fashion requires short development cycles, rapid prototyping, small batches 
and variety so that customers are offered the latest designs in limited quantities that 
ensure a sort of exclusivity.’ Shein has mastered ‘micro-batching,’ ordering as little as 50-
100 pieces from their suppliers at a time, and swiftly reordering if that particular SKU is 
successful so it can be put back on their online shelves 16. This extreme case of ‘just-in-
time’ strategy is risky, since due to the unusually low batch sizes, their suppliers often lose 
money on such orders. However, these losses are countered quickly, as popular products 
can be re-ordered straight away in as high of a quantity as is necessary. Thanks to Shein’s 
aligned supply chain, they have enormous amounts of control over their suppliers, and 
they support their factories with investment to build up their ‘small order quick response’ 
system. Shein unfortunately refuses to confirm information about its’ supplier network, but 
import records show that vi rtually all Shein’s ocean shipments to the US c ome from 
China17- another source states Shein insists their manufacturing contractors are all 
situated locally in the Chinese city of Guangzhou 16, which means they can manage them 
more easily because of the proximity.  This combined with their unique digitised  PAGE 4 
communication systems with automated algorithms, provides them with a short and tight 
supply chain that may be volatile, but it is one that they have full control over and allows 
their development cycle to be uniquely cheap and effective.  
Inditex also operates similarly, with lean production cycles and small batch sizes, however 
a key difference in the production end of their supply chain is that their suppliers are all 
over the world. 98% of their production is based in 12 countries (one of which is China), 
and almost all their clothing is sent to distribution centres in Spain. However, before the 
pandemic, a lot more of their production was based in China - the country was Inditex’ 
largest supplier, with 449 partners in 2018, an increase of 24 from the year before19. This 
began changing after the pandemic, as Zara began decoupling from China, and relying 
more on their other suppliers. According to Yogaananthan (2020) 20, to build a resilient 
supply chain post -covid, firms should diversify supply chains through multi -sourcing, as 
well as avoiding completely relying on China ; and Zara has followed both successfully.  
Meanwhile, Shein seems to rely solely on their home country for both production and 
distribution. Yoganaanthan also states that diversification complicates the supply chain 
and makes it more difficult to manage. Shein’s strategy of centralization  rather than 
diversification seems to work perfectly for them, and allows them more direct control and 
alignment over their supply chain. 
This may not be possible for firms based outside of China, though - especially after the 
pandemic. Covid was a contributor in intensifying political and financial tensions between 
China and the rest of the world, especially the US, in the form of tariff wars, import bans, 
and general distrust, which deteriorated trade relationships permanently 21. This resulted 
in difficulties for foreign firms such as Inditex, but in a way helped Shein develop. Inditex 
and other companies who ship all products in bulk from warehouses to retail stores, have 
no way of avoiding import/export taxes. Shein on the other hand,  manages distribution 
domestically, and exports individual customer orders from warehouses in China. In the 
US, the duty threshold on which imported packages are taxed is $800, meaning an 
average customer’s ‘#sheinhaul’ (a hashtag which has 14.6 billion views on TikTok 22) will 
not be taxed. As a result of this international trade war (which was largely stimulated by 
the “Chinese virus”), as well as support from their own government, Shein has been able 
to exploit tax loopholes, cutting costs on both imports and exports23. 
 
‘Finally, because most fast fashion retailers are publicly traded companies and their 
success is now measured by stock performance, they are increasingly under pressure to 
perform well on the stock markets.’ Inditex has been publicly traded since 2001, and Shein 
has very recently filed for a US IPO 24, despite in 2021 claiming to have ‘no IPO plans in 
the short term’23. This would be good news for their growth , as it would bring them major 
third-party investment. It would also force them to be more transpare nt with their supply 
chain and business practices- as a private firm, they are not complying with due diligence 
supply chain laws  to disclose any financial or operational information, and until recently 
have been deliberately secretive . The fashion industry in general is notorious for their 
questionable labour ethics, and Shein has particularly been under scrutiny for attempting 
to hide and deny theirs. Especially after the revolution in workplace health and safety and  PAGE 5 
labour laws due to the pandemic,  this will very likely require them to put more effort into 
making sure their workers are treated and paid fairly , and there has been increasing 
demand from potential investors, campaigners, and other shareholders for Shein to do so. 
This should prompt their supply chain to become more aligned with environmental, social 
and governance  management expectations, and make them a more sustainable and 
corporately responsible company.  
 
Conclusion  
The Covid-19 pandemic was an unprecedented shock to the whole economy, transforming 
all industries worldwide. In this era, the global fashion industry, represented by companies 
like Shein and Inditex, went through a litmus test that highlighted the importance of supply 
chains' resilience, adaptability, and agility. Unfortunately, many companies fell victim to 
this crisis and were not able to fully recover . Meanwhile for others it was an opportunity 
for new growth and expansion. 
Inditex did inevitably suffer from the supply and demand-side shocks, due to the disruption 
in international logisti cs which led to delays and backlogs , and the lockdowns which cut 
off an enormous quantity of sales from retail stores - an extreme example of the bullwhip 
effect in motion. However,  their agile supply chain allowed them to easily adapt by 
enhancing their existing online presence. Since most of their inventory was held 
strategically in centrali sed warehouses in Spain, this allowed them to simply  redirect 
shipments from retail stores to direct consumer delivery , without the need for 
reconsideration of their whole model.  
On the other hand, Shein is a case study on capitalising from a crisis. As a digital -first 
enterprise, they were entirely ready for this shift in consumer behaviour- it is possible that 
they were just at the right place at the right time. They did get a lot of things right, though, 
that many other online retailers did not. Not much is known about Chris Xu, the elusive 
CEO of Shein, but it is not surprising that he has a background in Search Engine 
Optimisation and is a marketing specialist. This sort of tec hnical expertise is largely what 
Shein owes their success to, as well as their clever marketing. The company’s main 
advantage over other online retailers was their integration of innovative algorithms and AI, 
whos’ growth was accelerated thanks to the pandemic,  to speed up and automate all 
aspects of its’ supply chain to levels no other fashion company has done before, displaying 
an advanced form of resilience. Unfortunately, the trade-off for these tactics was backlash, 
lawsuits, and allegations, and Shein’s denial and secrecy only fueled suspicion around 
their practices. 
These cases highlight some key implications for supply chain management in the face of 
external shocks , such as t he ability to pivot between sales channels to follow where  
demand leads, specifically realizing the power of e -commerce and digital platforms . As 
seen in Figure 1, the trend in the last 20 years is heading towards internet sales becoming 
the majority of total retail sales.  Evidence of this can also be seen in the form of high 
streets becoming increasingly empty over the last decade, with the pandemic being a last  PAGE 6 
nail in the coffin for some retailers. Of course, this shift is not as necessary or relevant for 
all industries, but this structural change is important to consider when making SCM 
decisions. 
However, is this a question of lack of resiliency, if a product or service you provide 
unexpectedly becomes obsolete? For example, is it fair to say Blockbuster was not ‘agile’ 
or ‘resilient’ enough for not becoming like Netflix? Was Topshop not agile enough for not 
developing an online shop earlier, and not expecting to have  to close their shops, almost 
overnight, if they were performing well and meeting expectations? Many retailers seemed 
to be over-reliant in their status as ‘kings of the high street’ 7, which may have given them 
a false sense of confidence and allowed management to put all their eggs in one baske t 
without sufficient ‘futureproofing’. I believe part of supply chain resilience is to expect the 
unexpected, and always be ready for the worst-case scenario. 
Lastly, ethical, environmental, and social issues  (ESG general) are becoming a hot topic 
across all industries. Unfortunately, no big corporation is innocent when it comes to this - 
increasing amounts of companies are being accused of either some sort of controversy , 
or at least ‘greenwashing ,’ to appear more sustainable than they really are - ‘opacity has 
become the norm’ 25. Shein is no stranger to this - until recently, they have made the 
deliberate decision to stay private, however they are recently considering trading publicly, 
which will open them to investors as wel l as forcing them to  be more transparent . They 
have committed to ‘reali se a fully circular fashion and textile industry by 2050’ 26, which 
sounds very vague, and could be another case of greenwashing. However, there seems 
to be societal changes coming, with increasing talk and protests about climate change 
and pollution , so these expectations could very well become requirements for supply 
chains globally. Assuming this is a genuine step in the right direction for Shein and the 
fast fashion industry, this could allow Shein to make it to Gartner’s Top 25 list one day.

What is ‘Fast Fashion’? 
It is difficult to pinpoint exactly when fast fashion became ‘fast .’ There is evidence that 
suggests humans first started sewing fabrics together using thin bones and rocks to make 
fitted pieces of clothing around 40,000 years ago 8. The history of the modern sewing 
machine is fairly recent, with many people claiming to have invented it around the 19 th 
century9. The way a sewing machine works is surprisingly complicated, but the exponential 
evolution of this technology in the last couple of centuries has revolutionised fashion, and 
allowed good quality clothing to be made very quickly, and helped fashion become 
incredibly accessible and affordable to anybody. Since the industrial revolution, demand 
for cheap, replaceable clothing has been steadily increasing at an enormous rate, and 
therefore people of all classes’ wardrobes have also been growing.   PAGE 7 
Nowadays, most clothing is mass -manufactured using automated production lines in 
factories, producing more than 100 billion items of clothing a year. China is the biggest 
powerhouse of these clothing factories, with around 65% of clothing being produced there. 
Additionally, thanks to the ‘third era of globalisation’ starting in 1989 10, these items of 
clothing can be exported to and from anywhere across the globe in a matter of days. As a 
result, the fashion industry has become one of the biggest industries, with very low barriers 
to entry to start a small clothing brand. However, to become a multi -billion-dollar brand 
like Inditex or Shein requires more than just creating, producing, and selling a couple of 
nice designs. An Agile, Adaptable, and Aligned supp ly chain is required to be able to 
manufacture and distribute the clothing (Lee, 2004), and this involves many 
interdependent moving parts across the globe.

The Winter Gritting Plan (Last Year) 
 
 
 
 
Overview 
 
The main element of winter gritting in Grantshire is the precautionary gritting of roads in anticipation of 
imminent freezing conditions to stop ice forming on the roadway. 
 
From an operational point of view, this involves having a set of vehicles and drivers that can spring into 
action very quickly, triggered by weather forecasts that anticipate freezing conditions.  
 
The main elements of such an ‘event’ are: 
 
• Mobilising 16 drivers and their gritsalt-spreading vehicles at the three depots in the County 
• Ensuring that the vehicles are loaded with the correct amount of spreading material (gritsalt) 
• Following the agreed spreading routes 
• Spreading the gritsalt in the appropriate quantities for the chosen roads on these routes 
• Returning to the depot to clean the vehicles 
  
In a typical winter, the number of gritting events is around 35 to 60 occasions. 
 
Historical data on events and temperatures is available for the last 59 years.  
 
In terms of timing, a ‘regular event’ sees the vehicles leave the depots at around 6pm and finish their routes 
by around 9pm. 
 
However, in particularly cold and/or windy situations the gritting is sometimes repeated in the early 
morning, usually around 5am, before most of the public start their journeys to work. This is referred to as a 
‘repeat event’. 
 
 
 
 
 
Planned Routes 
 
There are currently three depots in the County. The total roadway length in the County is 2,143 kilometres 
but not all of this is gritted. Also, there is the M6 motorway running through the southwest edge of the 
county but this is the responsibility of the Highways Authority and not the Local Authority – so it is not 
involved in the Alf’s winter maintenance plans.  
 
The current gritting routes cover 1,114 kilometres of actual roadway and 1,282 kilometres of road lanes 
(as some roads need to be gritted in both directions).  
 
The routes themselves have been determined using a routing algorithm. The algorithm finds the minimum 
total distance travelled by the 16 vehicles, given the constraints of the problem: the roads that need to be 
gritted, the capacity of the vehicles, the time available per route, driver workloads and so on.  
 
See figure 1.1 overleaf for a diagram of the 16 routes and three depots.

The government requires Authorities to report the road coverage percentage of their routes in terms of 
road length gritted divided by total road length – in this case around half (52%) of the roads in Grantshire 
are currently gritted. 
 
No specific targets are set and across England the overall average is 38% with a high of 75% and a low of 
20%. The National Audit Office recommends a minimum of 35%. Hence, from this perspective, the coverage 
in Grantshire is clearly acceptable. 
 
The average lane length gritted per route is around 80 kilometres with a high of 90 kilometres and a low of 
67 kilometres.  
 
 
Within any individual vehicle route there are two types of ‘mileage’; gritting mileage and dead mileage. 
‘Gritting mileage’ is where the vehicle is ejecting gritsalt onto the road and ‘dead mileage’ is when the vehicle 
is driving but no gritsalt is being ejected.  
 
Dead mileage occurs for three reasons: 
 
1. The vehicle has only just left the depot but hasn’t yet reached the start of its designated gritting route 
2. The vehicle is driving on a road that has already been gritted previously, by either another vehicle or that 
same vehicle 
3. The vehicle is travelling down a minor road that isn’t designated to be gritted (this is rare though). 
 
The total gritting mileage per event is 1,282 km, and the total dead mileage per event is 368 km, meaning 
the total mileage (gritting plus dead) covered per event is 1,650 kilometres.

Gritting Fleet and Gritsalt Usage 
 
Last season the Authority operated 16 gritting vehicles of 10.5 tonnes (of gritsalt) capacity, except two 
older vehicles which hold slightly more (11). One very old vehicle is also held in reserve, in case of an 
emergency breakdown.  
 
The average width of the road lanes gritted in Grantshire is 7.2 metres and the spreading rate is computer-
controlled in terms of grams per metres squared. For precautionary gritting this Authority currently spreads 
at 15 grams per square metre, which is somewhat higher than the recommended minimum of 10 grams per 
square metre on the roadway as some material is wasted in the spreading process: for example, it can 
bounce or be blown into the verges. 
 
During an average winter season, the Authority uses around 6,000 tonnes of gritsalt for precautionary 
gritting. The capacity of Grantshire’s stockpile across 3 depots is around 7,000 tonnes. Should Grantshire 
run out of gritsalt then there is the facility to order more, but the price is always higher than usual during 
winter due to demand effects (budget for £35 per tonne).  
 
Furthermore, there is a very small chance that national supplies of gritsalt could run out completely, thus 
making re-stocking impossible (or at the least very problematic). This has never happened though.

3. An increase in the total gritting distance per event, from 1,282 km to 1,333 km, due to new road building

The Properties of Salt and Other Materials for Winter Gritting 
 
John Thornton 
 
June 2019 
 
Highway salt – also referred to as gritsalt or rock salt – is used in large quantities around the world to keep 
roads clear of ice and snow.   
 
In the Unites States approximately 15 million tonnes of salt are spread each winter – a figure that has 
increased from an average of 10 million tonnes in the 1980s.   
 
Salt is relatively cheap to buy ($40 per tonne in the US and £20-25 per tonne in the UK) and other potential 
de-icing chemicals are much more expensive.  Vitaliano (1992)4 looked at the use of Calcium Magnesium 
Acetate (CMA) in the US as an alternative which was priced at $650 per tonne at that time.  
 
Although salt is relatively inexpensive, readily available and effective, it does have the unfortunate side 
effects of being environmentally unfriendly, and is damaging to both metallic infrastructure due to corrosion 
and concrete due to spalling. 
 
However, substantial capital has been invested in developing a salt supply, distribution and deployment 
infrastructure. Therefore if additives are available, at a reasonable cost that militates against such 
deleterious effects the resultant product may be seen as holistically more cost-effective and operationally 
elegant as an effective winter maintenance material.  
 
In England gritsalt sales in very cold winters can reach 2 million tonnes but the average is closer to one 
million tonnes per winter.  
 
Gritsalt is normally composed of at least 90% sodium chloride, 2% to 4% water and the remaining 
constituents are insoluble particles that give extra traction and anti-caking agents to keep the salt friable and 
easy to spread. Gritsalt is normally spread as 6 mm or 10 mm particles.  
 
Although there have been other chemicals used on the UK road network, for example Urea on the Midland 
Links elevated sections, gritsalt has completely dominated the market since it was introduced in the early 
1960s.  Most other counties in Europe use wetted salt or brine but this has never caught on in the UK as ‘dry’ 
gritsalt is normally able to go into solution when spread, due to the high humidity in the UK’s maritime 
climate.  In drier climates, getting the salt to go into solution can be a problem.   
 
 
Corrosion Costs 
 
Vehicle Corrosion 
 
Today most new cars are supplied in the UK with extended (6 to 10 years) corrosion warranty guarantees.  
This covers any corrosion to the car bodywork but does not normally cover corrosion to car exhausts.   
 
Vehicle corrosion due to salt has been estimated by TRL at around £200 million per annum in England which 
is the equivalent of £8 per annum of corrosion for each of the 25 million vehicles due to salt. It also equates 
to approximately £200 per annum per tonne of salt spread.

Accidents on Roads that are not subject to Precautionary Salting 
 
 
It is not possible to say with certainty how accidents rates compare on roads that are subject to planned 
precautionary salting in relation to those roads not so covered because road accident statistics have not 
been collected in this way. 
 
For England as a whole the overall coverage of the winter gritting programme in terms of the proportion of 
Local Authority road kilometres covered is around 38% and, hence, 62% are unsalted. Since the principal-A 
roads (always salted) account for around 9% of the total road length, on average, only 29% (38% minus 
9%) of the minor roads are covered by salting programmes, and therefore 71% of the minor roads are not 
salted. 
 
Thus – if accidents occur in the same ratio – we can say that up to 71% of the minor road accidents (71% of 
93,639 = 66,484) could have occurred on roads that are not subject to precautionary salting. 
 
An unpublished survey of ten Local Authorities carried out by the Audit Commission in their review of 
coverage rates found that in this sample around 9% of the rural minor roads received precautionary salting 
but that around 35% of the urban minor roads were covered. This result suggests that an urban minor road 
is around 3.89 times more likely to receive salting treatment than a rural minor road.  
 
In England as a whole, there are 101,414 km of urban minor roadway and 86,946 km of rural minor 
roadway: a total of 188,360 kilometres. By applying the 29% coverage of minor roads we obtain an estimate 
of 54,624 km of minor roads are salted. And thus 133,736km of unsalted minor roads.

The Contribution of Icy Conditions to Accidents 
 
 
• A German Study 
 
The only direct study of the effects of road gritting on accidents on rural roads has been in Germany carried 
out by the Darmstadt Technical University (OECD 1989)5 and this work concluded that the accident rate in 
the four hours before salting was 3.65 times the rate following salting. This study further concluded that in 
relation to rural roads in Germany around 15 % of all accidents are directly affected by whether or not the 
roads involved are included in a planned salting programme. 
 
 
• Official Statistics on Road Conditions and Accidents 
 
The STATS19 data in England (Department for Transport) does include information intended to reflect the 
contributions of road conditions to accidents. However there are significant difficulties in interpreting these 
data.  
 
The data from the STATS19 database suggests that a maximum of around 8% of all reported accidents might 
be directly influenced by ‘slippery’ road conditions.  
 
This would imply that 223 fatalities, 1,990 serious injury accidents and 12,783 slight injury accidents 
(totalling 14,996) in the survey year (2019) in England could have been so affected.  
 
If the assumption were to be made that all such accidents are on unsalted roads, this would translate into a 
25.5% effect on the unsalted roads (14,996 ÷ 58,841). However, not all ‘slippery’ accidents are the result of 
ice, not all reported ‘slippery’ conditions necessarily contributed to the actual accident and not all such 
accidents occurred on roads not subject to precautionary salting. 
 
 
• A Conservative Estimate 
 
Overall the German result is perhaps the most robust basis for assessing the accident reduction effects of 
salting since it was a direct study of the effect. This German study estimated that 15% of all accidents are 
affected by the winter gritting activity whereas the STATS19 data suggests a maximum of 25.5%. 
 
In the cost benefit analysis in the next section the more conservative estimate of 10% has been applied. 
Given the complex nature of many accidents, with many contributing factors, a value of 10% is seen as a 
reasonable value to use.

Optimizing Grantshire’s Gritting Service: A 
Comprehensive Analysis of Grantshire’s Gritting Depot 
Development and Relocation Options 
 
Executive Summary 
 
In this report, we present a thorough analysis of options for the development or relocation of 
Grantshire Council's gritting depots. In our analysis we focus on efficiency and cost-
effectiveness, while keeping public safety as a main priority. After evaluating logistical 
considerations, accident rates on different road types and operational costs under varying 
weather conditions, our ultimate recommendation is option 6b. We have determined depot Z 
to be the best option for its robust responsiveness to harsh weather conditions, while 
minimising environmental impact and maximising resource utilisation. This is due to its 
central positioning, which provides the most cost-effective solution to the problem of putting 
salt on the roads through limiting the dead mileage on all the routes. Additionally, a brand-
new depot encourages investment in technology and infrastructure to improve fleet 
longevity, which will further enhance Grantshire’s ability to ensure safe road conditions for 
the foreseeable future. By considering our recommendations, Grantshire can effectively 
safeguard the wellbeing of its’ citizens, and optimise road maintenance operations 
throughout this investment life cycle.

3. Gritting strategy 
3.1 Prioritisation by Road Type 
In Grantshire, around half (52%) of roads are currently gritted. The National Audit Office 
recommends a minimum of 35%, and across England the overall average is 38% with a high 
of 75%. This percentage is more than acceptable from this perspective, as Grantshire exceeds 
the recommended minimum as well as the national average. This extensive coverage likely 
contributes to lower accident rates compared to other regions, ultimately helping keep 
Grantshire’s roads safer than the rest of the nation on average.

According to relative accident rates in terms of traffic volumes ( measure in billion vehicle

fatal accidents are rural minor roads and principal A roads, therefore these are a priority for 
gritting. In England as a whole, around 88.65% of rural minor roads are unsalted, compared 
to 55.87% of urban minor roads. Because of this, we would recommend targeting more rural 
roads as there is significant room for improvement, especially considering how dangero us

The spreading rate is set to 15g/m 2, which is above the recommended minimum of 10g/m 2. 
This suggests an effort to maximise effectiveness of each event, as some material gets wasted 
by getting blown away off the road, for example. If it was necessary, for example to cut costs, 
then there is space to decrease the spreading rate so that it would still be within the 
recommended amounts. There is nothing to suggest that increasing the spreading rate would 
add any benefit, apart from simply being more costly. There is an argument to be made that 
less salt should be used, as it causes corrosion to metallic infrastructure, concrete and 
vehicles. However, the costs of these are minimal in comparison to the financial and social 
costs of accidents caused by not gritting roads enough.  
 
3.2 Gritting depot capacity and costs 
We also broke down the numbers on the amount of grit needed across each type of weather 
conditions. For an average winter we would use just over 6,000 tonnes of grit- all options are 
able to hold this amount therefore none will be ruled out. However, for a harsh winter we 
estimated to use just over 8600 tonnes of grit. This exceeds the capacity of any of the depots. 
Therefore, we would need to factor in how easy it is to reorder grit and how accessible it is to 
deliver to the depots. Using two depots may be inferior to using just one, as in a harsh winter 
we will need to restock grit and may be on short notice. Delivering to two different depots may 
cause problems  with distributing the material across the  trucks in each depot. However, 
delivering to one depot may be more convenient as all the grit will be stored in one place and 
be accessible for all the trucks. 
 
During an average winter season, the Authority uses around 6,000 tonnes of grit salt for 
precautionary gritting. The depot capacity is 7,000 tonnes, which leaves a buffer of around 
1,000 tonnes on average. Last season 5,463 tonnes were used over 38 events, therefore the 
stockpile was more than enough. However, last season was relatively mild so this may not be 
the case every year. If we had another winter like in 1967/68 which had the highest number 
of events since 1965 with 68 events, we would need nearly 10,000 tonnes of grit salt, which 
could cost over £250,000 on salt alone. This would go way over the stockpile capacity and 
force us to order at least 2/3,000 extra tonnes at the higher price of £35 a tonne. This also 
bears the practical risks of shipment delays due to extreme weather conditions, or the small 
chance of re-stocking becoming problematic. This has never happened yet, and 1967/68 was 
an extreme example. However, these sorts of extreme weather events may become more 
frequent due to climate change, so increasing the stockpile capacity may be worth considering 
if weather trends suggest more frequent harsh winters in the future. 
 
Looking further at the costs for grit, on a low end a tonne of grit would cost £25 and on the 
high end it would cost £35. From our grit values for a harsh and average winter we were able 
to determine that the low-end cost for grit in a harsh winter is £215,640 and for high end cost  it would be £301,896, which is a 40% difference in cost. This is a substantial jump in price- we 
can infer over a long period of time the additional cost of purchasing grit for £35 would be 
significant. Over a 30-year period we see the difference of costs rise to just over £2,500,000. 
Therefore, in order to have a cost -efficient model for the whole operation we would need to 
minimise our operational cost to balance out t he cost of grit if it was bought at the high end. 
Using the most cost -efficient option to tackle the gritting problem could allow investment 
elsewhere.   
 
4. Gritter availability and operational effectiveness 
Investing in upgrading and maintaining our fleet of gritting trucks is essential in ensuring 
operational effectiveness during winter seasons. With this investment, we can enhance the 
quality of maintenance and overall availability of gritters, while optimising their performance to 
meet the demands of varying weather conditions. Focusing on the longevity of this investment 
allows us to take advantage of technological advancements and incorporate these into options 
such as 6B, where we can tailor the depot from the ground up to ensure all of Grantshire’s 
needs can be met over the long term. 
 
Addressing breakdowns and maintenance issues promptly is crucial for minimising disruptions 
to our gritting operations. Centralising our resources by establishing a new depot in location Z 
streamlines our response to breakdowns. By consolidating  spare gritters and maintenance 
equipment in a single location, we can improve our fleet's responsiveness , mobility and 
longevity. This centralised approach enhances our ability to quickly address breakdowns, 
ensuring that our gritting trucks remain operational and ready to tackle winter weather 
conditions effectively. 
 
As we make this long -term investment in our gritting infrastructure, it's essential to maintain 
flexibility in our capacity for grit salt and gritters. Regardless of the chosen depot location, we 
must keep the option of purchasing more gritters open , in order to accommodate potential 
expansion and evolving operational needs. By maintaining flexibility in our capacity for grit salt 
and gritters, we can adapt to changing demands and ensure that our gritting operations remain 
robust and effective over time. This approach allows us to future-proof our infrastructure and 
optimise our ability to respond to all types of winter weather conditions effecting Grantshire. 
 
5. Cost analysis 
5.1 Initial cost analysis  
 
The potential cost of each option is a key consideration, especially given the council is looking 
to ensure any investment it makes has sufficient returns. After receiving the closing, running 
and initial costs for all the options, we found option 6 a to have the lowest running costs at 
£20,000, beating the competition by 24%. This suggests that this option would be the cheapest 
in the long term. 
 
However, we also had to factor in the initial and clos ing costs which saw an overall cost to 
start up being £268,000 for this option. This value calculated is on the high end of the scale 
when compared with other options, due to the fact that we would need to close current depots 
and open a brand new one. Similarly, option 6b also has a low running cost of £25,000 and 
overall start-up cost of £318,000. This anal ysis makes us confident that either of these two 
options would be the best long-term investment if the council has a heavy focus on reducing 
recurring monthly expenses. 
  We wanted to look at the operational costs under different eventualities to see the most cost-
efficient model, as over a long period of time there is a high chance of a potential change in 
weather conditions. This has especially been the case recently with the true extent of climate 
change being realised. To factor these changing weather conditions into our analy sis we did 
three sets of different calculations for our operational cost.  
 
5.2 Cost analysis under differing weather conditions 
 
First, we wanted to find what we could consider an average winter by looking at past data of 
how many events would normally occur each year. We calculated an average over several 
different time periods so we could gather a good estimate of occurrences. Add itionally we 
calculated averages over 12 and 18 years, to capture possible trends that didn't occur in recent 
times, and such a long average would filter out outliers which will give us a more suitable and 
representative value for our events. We found the average values were between 41 and 42 
and therefore took an average winter to be 42 events to be conservative. 
  
From this we could calculate the operational cost for an average winter using our costing 
model. We also considered additional driver costs in the calculations to give us a complete 
overall operational cost. After adding the additional drivers’ costs, we s ee 6b and 1 become 
the two most cost -efficient options at different points in time. Breaking it down to better 
understand this performance, these two options have the lowest additional driver cost, 
indicating that when prolonging the drivers journey by add ing additional mileage on to the 
route, we don’t benefit financially. Over a short period of time, we see option 1 being the most 
cost efficient with option 2 being in close second with just over a £30,000 difference over 5 
years, this is due to the low start up and closing costs. After 20 years we see the low running 
and operational costs of our new depots becoming influential as option 6b and 6b close the 
overall cost gap. After 30 years we see option 6b and 1 only separated by a few hundred 
thousand pounds. This most cost -efficient solution over a 30 -year period was 6b as costs 
came to £13,815,563. As expected, due to their low running costs one of the new depots 
became the most cost-efficient option over a longer period. However a factor not considered 
was the repair of equipment which is more likely to fail in the older depots which are expanding, 
as our new sites will have the new technology and the machines are more likely to be durable. 
  
Secondly, we calculated costs for a mild winter to understand the operations under a best -
case scenario. A value of 35 was used as this was the l owest number of events for a single 
year on record. Our findings were similar to the previously stated average winter conditions, 
where again we see, over a long period of time, our options for new depots becoming the most 
cost-efficient. Our calculations under a mild winter show option 1 being the cheapest over 30 
years with a value of £9,902,000, with 6b close behind with only a £61,000 difference. 
 
Finally, we calculated costs for a harsh winter, which was intended to show the worst scenario 
possible and how each option would perform under these conditions. This could be very useful 
for future-proofing the decision and ensuring the option picked coul d perform well under all 
eventualities. This is particularly important considering the context where, if underprepared for 
a harsh winter, the safety of the coun ty’s citizens could come under threat on icy roads. We 
suggested a harsh winter would contain 6 8 events, as this was the maximum events that 
occurred in a single year from across the past data. Once again, we saw similar results where 
over a short period of time option 1 and 2 are the most cost effective, whereas over a long 
period of time option 6b becomes superior and the most cost efficient. For a single year of 68 
events the cheapest operational costs come to £476,142 which is option 6b, £7,800 cheaper 
than option 1 in second. Over 30 years including the initial costs we still have these two options 
being the cheapest with both being just over £14,600,000. However, it must be noted that this 
is the worst scenario possible and is therefore very unlikely to repeat consistently.    
 
6. Conclusion 
 
In conclusion, our analysis of the potential development and or relocation of the Grantshire 
Council grit salt depots provides useful insights into the optimisation of the winter operations 
which can allow the decision makers to make well informed decisions.  
 
The consideration of human and environmental logistical factors details the importance of 
employee workload management and the minimisation of environmental impacts such as 
dead mileage. The option 6B performed particularly well in these areas, showcasing its 
potential to enhance operational efficiency while reducing environmental footprint. 
 
Understanding the impact each type of road has on accident rates we found to be another key 
consideration, particularly rural minor roads, and principal A roads due to their higher accident 
rates. This highlights the importance of targeting gritting strate gies to ensure the highest 
possible level of road safety whilst using the least possible resources. Despite Grantshire's 
gritting coverage surpassing national recommendations, there is a lot of space for 
improvement, especially in targeting rural areas whe re significant safety enhancements can 
be achieved.  
 
Furthermore, the analysis of gritting depot capacity and costs reveals the necessity of 
balancing operational efficiency with financial considerations. Options like 6b emerge as cost-
effective solutions, particularly under harsh winter scenarios, demonstrating the value of new 
investment in infrastructure and the improvements it can make to the level of efficiency. 
 
The consideration of operational costs under differing weather conditions is key as its 
emphasis must be put on future-proofing decisions giving the level of investment and ensuring 
cost-efficiency over the long term. By integrating new technological advan cements, and 
improving capacity planning, Grantshire can ensure its gritting operations remain robust and 
effective in mitigating the impacts of winter weather conditions long into the future. 
 
Considering these findings, the final recommendations prioritise options that offer the best 
balance between operational efficiency, cost -effectiveness, and safety considerations which 
are key to the council. By adopting a comprehensive approach that addresses both immediate 
needs and long -term sustainability, Grantshire can optimise its gritting operations to better 
serve its community and ensure safer road conditions during winter months.  
 
7. Final recommendations 
After analysing and evaluating all our options concerning the development or relocation of 
Grantshire’s grit salt depots, option 6B emerged as the optimal choice. Despite initial startup 
costs, its long-term operational efficiency outweighs these expenses, in large part due to its 
central position; ensuring minimal dead -mileage, rapid responsiveness to brea kdowns and 
resilience to different weather scenarios including  the more severe winters Grantshire may 
face in the future. This reliability while tackling a harsh winter while also having the cheapest 
operational cost of any of the options makes 6B the best value for money over time, ideal for 
a long-term investment such as this.  
 
Adding to this, with 6B being a completely new depot , investment can be put into the 
technology built into it to further optimise everything from gritter maintenance to a potentially 
more suitable grit salt capacity that ensures Grantshire is stocked up and can avoid re-ordering  where possible. Furthermore, the advantages of building a centralised gritting depot from the 
ground up stretch to the availability and longevity of our gritting fleet, leaving us the option to 
expand the fleet as well as  having all spare parts and mechani cs on one modern site , 
increasing the quality and speed of any repairs that may need to be carried out.  
 
By adopting these recommendations and selecting Option 6b, Grantshire  can ensure robust 
and reliable gritting operations, effectively safeguarding the well-being of its’ citizens.

2.1 Space 
Spacing was an important consideration with the creation of the survey  as having 
appropriate designs in a survey impacts quality of responses gathered as respondents 
can easily understand questions and the survey itself (Ball, 2019). The fonts, colour 
scheme and layout of the survey was considered hence the justification for the usage of 
google forms was used due to the simplicity of the layout and the easy conversion to excel 
data to assist with completing part c. of brief 4 . Furthermore, the usage of google forms 
allows for a URL link to be generated allowing for accessibility for participants. The data 
collection methodology to prove/disprove the hypothesis involves random sampling 
using a Google Forms survey to gather data associate d with the two main variables of 
electric scooter affordability and accessibility. To gather participants, the survey will be 
spread through a URL link to individuals who go to university such as group chats with 
students and individuals who study within Pamplona.  
 
2.2 Time 
The timing was an important factor when the survey was sent to group chats as well as to 
people who survived in the field. Certain factors such as when people were surveyed 
influence the overall quality of responses an example involves asking for someone t o 
complete a survey late at night where individuals will not be as engaged as someone 
during the middle of the day (Estelami, 2014). The survey was constructed with the 
consideration of allowing participants to complete the survey in a reasonable time 
without the participant getting disengaged due to a lengthy survey. This consideration 
resulted in the survey having 14 questions to keep respondents engaged (Estelami, 2014). 
Regarding the posting of the survey in group chats and participants, the timing was an 
important factor in when the survey was sent oftentimes, consisting during the middle of 
the day to ensure that the largest group of individuals would view the survey. Additionally, 
Furthermore, there were cases (<7 Individuals) where data was sourced in the field before 
and after class without sending a URL to a group chat. This may have created potential 
biases and timing and space issues regarding the sourcing of data as respondents may 
not have been as focused on the survey but instead on the upcomin g class or tired after

3 General Report 
As urban landscapes evolve and sustainability takes center  stage, electric scooters (e -
scooters) are emerging as a modern solution to the challenges of urban transportation. 
This report examines the feasibility of introducing BODR e -scooters to Pamplona, 
focusing on the city’s large university student population.  With its compact size, young 
demographic, and increasing focus on sustainable transport, Pamplona presents a 
promising market for BODR’s entry. However, understanding the commuting habits, 
perceptions, and potential barriers faced by students is essential  to develop a tailored 
strategy that ensures success. 
The research process began by defining the core objective: assessing whether university 
students in Pamplona would adopt e -scooters as an alternative mode of transport. To 
address this question, the study aimed to understand students’ commuting preferences, 
their attitudes toward e -scooters, and the barriers they perceive to adoption. The 
 16 
 
methodology employed a combination of quantitative and qualitative approaches, 
ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the target market. 
The primary method of data collection was a survey distributed both online and in person 
to students at the University of Navarra. With over 70 respondents, the survey explored 
topics such as current commuting habits, infrastructure perceptions, financial 
considerations, and openness to adopting e -scooters. Complementing this data were 
five focus groups, which provided qualitative insights into student attitudes, including 
discussions on safety, affordability, and the practicality of using e-scooters in Pamplona. 
Finally, secondary data from industry reports and demographic studies added depth to 
the analysis, allowing the findings to be placed in a broader market context. 
Once collected, the data underwent a meticulous cleaning process to ensure reliability. 
Frivolous or unrealistic responses, such as “teleportation” as a commuting method, were 
excluded from the analysis. The cleaned dataset was categorized, highlighting trends and 
recurring themes, while focus group discussions were transcribed and thematically 
coded. This systematic approach ensured that the findings were robust and actionable. 
The results of the study revealed valuable insights into the commuting behaviors and 
preferences of university students in Pamplona. Walking emerged as the dominant mode 
of transportation, with approximately 70% of respondents identifying it as their prima ry 
method of commuting. This was largely attributed to proximity, as many students live 
within a 10 -20 minute radius of the university. For those living farther away, buses were 
the next most popular choice, followed by cycling. E-scooters were rarely used, with most 
respondents citing limited access and high costs as deterrents. These findings suggest 
that while walking and buses currently dominate, e -scooters have the potential to fill a 
gap for students with longer or less convenient commutes. 
When asked about Pamplona’s infrastructure, students provided mixed reviews. Public 
transport infrastructure received an average rating of 3.8 out of 5, with many respondents 
appreciating the availability of bike lanes and frequent bus services. However, a  lack of 
docking and storage facilities for shared mobility options was noted as a significant 
limitation. In contrast, infrastructure for e-scooters received a slightly lower score of 3.4 
out of 5. Students highlighted issues such as insufficient parking spaces, limited charging 
points, and difficulties navigating older parts of the city. These results indicate that while 
Pamplona has a solid foundation for e -scooter use, targeted improvements in 
infrastructure could significantly enhance their viability. 
Financial considerations emerged as a major barrier to adoption. On average, 
respondents rated their financial situation at 3.2 out of 5, reflecting moderate affordability. 
When asked about their willingness to pay for an e -scooter, over 50% of respondents  
preferred a price range of €100 -200, while only a small proportion were willing to spend 
over €300. This sensitivity to price underscores the importance of affordability in  17 
 
influencing adoption. To address this, BODR could consider offering entry -level e -
scooters within the €150-200 range or introducing flexible payment plans. Additionally, a 
digital renting system, like shared e-bike platforms, could be highly effective. A proposed 
rental fee of €2 per hour, or €25 for unlimited monthly use, would provide an accessible 
option for students, particularly those hesitant to commit to an outright purchase. 
Despite these challenges, there is clear interest in e -scooters among students. 
Approximately 40% of respondents expressed a willingness to consider purchasing an e-
scooter, with convenience and time savings cited as the primary motivators. However, 
safety concerns and the lack of adequate infrastructure were frequently mentioned as 
barriers. Sustainability, while appreciated as a secondary benefit, was not a primary 
driver for most students. Instead, practicality and affordability took precedence. 
The findings align with the study’s objectives and provide valuable insights into the 
potential for BODR e -scooters in Pamplona. However, the research also highlighted 
several limitations. The sample was skewed toward students living near the university, 
potentially underrepresenting those with longer commutes. Additionally, the study 
focused exclusively on Pamplona, limiting its generalizability to other regions. Finally, the 
short duration of the study constrained the depth of data collection, and the 
sustainability-related questions could have been more detailed. 
Looking ahead, future research should address these limitations. Expanding the 
geographic scope to include other cities with similar demographics would provide 
comparative insights. Conducting longitudinal studies could track the evolution of 
commuting behaviours and e -scooter adoption over time. Moreover, a pilot program in 
Pamplona, offering both purchase and rental options, would provide valuable real-world 
data on adoption barriers and motivators. 
Based on the findings, several recommendations can be made. BODR should focus on 
affordability by offering budget-friendly e-scooters and introducing a digital rental system. 
Collaborating with local authorities to improve docking, parking, and charging 
infrastructure would address key barriers. Safety campaigns, including workshops and 
instructional materials, could build user confidence. Marketing efforts should emphasize 
the convenience and time savings of e -scooters for long -distance commuters while 
positioning sustainability as a complementary benefit. Finally, a pilot program would 
allow BODR to test its strategy, refine its offerings, and build awareness within the student 
community. 
In conclusion, this study demonstrates significant potential for BODR e-scooters to meet 
the commuting needs of university students in Pamplona. While challenges such as 
affordability and infrastructure limitations exist, these can be effectively addressed  
through targeted strategies. By offering flexible pricing models, leveraging a digital renting 
platform, and working with local stakeholders, BODR can successfully position itself as  18 
 
a leader in sustainable urban mobility. With thoughtful planning and ongoing research, 
BODR has the opportunity to make a meaningful impact in Pamplona’s transportation 
landscape.

At an altitude of 4,200 metres in the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, Colombia, Edilsa Ibañéz Ibañéz 
lowers a cupped hand into the water of a glacial stream. A local guide and mountaineer, she 
has grown up drinking water that runs down from the snowy peaks above. As she stands up, 
however, the landscape that greets her is markedly different from that of her childhood. “We 
used to think the ice would be eternal,” says Ibañéz, 45. “Now it is not so eternal. Our glaciers 
are dying.” 
The Sierra Nevada del Cocuy is one of six remaining glaciers in Colombia. Although it has lost 
more than 90% of its ice since the second half of the 19th century, Ibañéz says it contains 
about 36% of the country’s total glacial coverage. 
Swathes of dry rock are exposed in areas once carpeted in snow in the high Sierra Nevada 
peaks. On the trail leading to the Cóncavo peak, stone markers have been placed like 
gravestones to indicate the position of the snow line in years past. The farthest marker, dating 
from the end of the 19th century, is several kilometres from the nearest ice. 
The peak itself presents a similarly grim picture. Fingers of greying ice slide towards the rocky 
mass below, where frozen boulders soften and thaw in the harsh sun. Deep within the glacier, 
the shifting ice emits loud cracks that rattle through the thin air above. 
SUBHEADING (Arial Bold 9 pt type size / 11 pt leading): Facing irreversible losses  Although the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy is home to the largest glacial mass in the country, it is 
far from alone in its fate. Rising global temperatures and increasingly unpredictable weather 
patterns are devastating all six of Colombia’s remaining glaciated areas. In 2024, neighbouring 
Venezuela became the first country in modern history to lose all its glaciers, and some predict 
that Colombia could go the same way in as little as 30 years. 
“Even if we were to very aggressively over the next 10 to 20 years reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions, it wouldn’t be enough,” says Mathias Vuille, a professor of atmospheric and 
environmental sciences at the University at Albany, who has been studying the climate crisis in 
the Andes for more than 30 years. “They aren’t accumulating any fresh snow and ice any more 
– they are doomed.” 
Colombia’s lowest-lying glacier, Santa Isabel in Los Nevados national park, far west of the 
Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, will probably be the first to disappear. According to data from the 
Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (Ideam), it will probably be 
gone within five years. 
Matteo Giraldo, 32, from the nearby city of Pereira, has been walking in the mountains around 
Santa Isabel for the past 16 years. “I’ve cried for the situation with the glacier,” he says. “To 
see it before and after has been something I’ve felt in my heart.” Along with others who have 
frequented the glacier in recent decades, Giraldo has seen firsthand the changes that caused 
one section, Conejeras, to disappear entirely between December 2023 and February 2024. 
The loss of Colombia’s glaciers poses a ticking timebomb for those living in the country’s high-
altitude regions. Vuille says: “Glaciers are constantly melting in the tropics – that means they 
constantly release water. That’s why they are essential, like a reservoir. It is your only water 
source if you live very close to the glacier.” 
SUBHEADING (Arial Bold 9 pt type size / 11 pt leading): A vulnerable source of water 
The ability of glaciers to retain and release vast quantities of water makes them a vital source 
for communities living across the Andes. The Sierra Nevada del Cocuy alone contains the 
equivalent of about 256,000 Olympic swimming pools of water. 
Unlike their counterparts in higher-latitude regions, such as Europe and North America, 
Colombia’s tropical glaciers are relatively constant in temperature. This results in a shorter 
period of ice accumulation and a longer, year-round period of water release. People living in 
Colombia’s mountains rely heavily on the swiftly diminishing glaciers for their main water 
supply. 
Ibañéz and her relatives, who live at the foot of the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy, consider 
themselves part of this group. “Very soon, we will be the first to run out of water,” she says. 
“Most people here aren’t aware of this.”

An exploration of transparency and 
looking through things
Michal Kosnik This collection of photographs aims 
to explore the idea of transparency, 
translucency and opacity, and what it 
means to look through ‘see-through’ 
media in order to see whats on the 
other side- as well as some visual 
effects that can happen as a result 
of doing so.
The photos are roughly in order 
of how abstractly this notion is 
interpreted.
Usual transparent objects, like a 
window or a glass of water, will allow 
light to pass through relatively 
clearly, allowing you to see what 
is on the other side of them.
Sometimes the ‘see-through’ object 
is in fact only semi-transparent, 
or translucent, and obscures or 
distorts the object on the other 
side in one way or another. Other times, an object between the 
viewer and another object isn’t 
transparent or translucent at all, 
yet we can still ‘see through’ it- 
for example when the intermediary 
object is not solid. 
This results in two opaque objects, 
one in front of the other, that are 
both within our view- this can create 
a harmonious visual relationship 
between the two.
This compilation is a visual 
investigation, and at times, an 
attempt to push the boundaries of 
what it means to look, or see, 
through objects of different levels 
of opacity. This can be interpreted 
as a relationship between foreground 
and background.

Project 3. Energy consumption modelling 
 
Suppose you are a dynamic team of data analysts and project managers who are working for a 
research institute in the Sustainable Country. In this nation, there is a strong commitment to a 
greener, more sustainable future, and developing an effective energy consumption management 
stands as a top priority.  
The ability to model energy consumption and use these models to estimate future energy needs is 
paramount. Underestimating demand could lead to devastating outages that impact lives and the 
nation's economy. On the other hand, overestimating could result in idle capacity, wasting valuable 
financial resources. 
The objective of the project that your team is working on is to develop an energy demand model 
that can estimate and forecast future energy needs within the residential sector of the Sustainable 
Country. This model will serve as a vital tool for policy makers and energy-related organisations. To 
achieve this, your project employs multiple regression analysis. You will examine various factors that 
influence residential energy consumption, including resident population, GDP, household size, 
median household income, and the costs of residential electricity, etc. The developed model will not 
only facilitate a sustainable and reliable energy supply but also contribute to the nation's vision of a 
greener future. 
Your tasks are the following: 
• Use a country of your choice and think about it as it were the Sustainable Country. Give 
some explanation as to why you have selected this country. 
• Identify the factors that influence the residential energy consumption. Use a literature 
search to find this out.  
• Use secondary data sources to collect historical data about these independent variables 
along with the dependent variable for the model. 
• Evaluate the nature of the relationship between each independent variable and the 
dependent variable. 
• Construct a few different models and test that they satisfy the assumptions of the multiple 
regression model. 
• Discuss the results of your analysis and compare them with the findings in the literature. 
• Use the developed model to forecast the residential energy consumption for a five-year 
period. 
• Comment on the limitations of the model and discuss the ways in which it could be 
improved. 
• Provide recommendations for policymakers to effectively utilise the project's findings. 
 
Before you embark on the project, you will need to work on the project outline. The guidelines are 
provided in a separate document.

Group E
Residential Energy 
consumption modelling Our task was to model how domestic energy usage has changed over time in 
the UK and forecast it for the next 5 years.
To achieve this we studied and analysed the last 35 years of government and 
public data on energy consumption and household income to create an 
accurate multiple regression model.
This is important because over the last 5 years energy prices have fluctuated 
wildly due to geopolitical uncertainty and conflict. These factors heavily affect 
the price of gas and electricity causing stress on the UK’s energy infastructure 
contributing to a cost of living crisis.
Therefore, this forecast is important because It will help shape the Uk’s energy 
policy allowing it to de -risk and ease the transition to renewable and 
sustainable sources.
Introduction Project Goals:
• Create a multiple regression 
model
• Create an accurate 5 year 
forecast 
• Ensure our model is robust 
and has minimal 
multicolinearity
• Provide accurate policy and 
economic recommendations 
based on multiple different 
scenarios
Project Overview
Project Scope:
• The model is only domestic 
data so Industrial data is not 
included
• We have taken a top down 
approch to modelling data 
so seasonal fluctuations 
have not been analysed.
• We have only used data from 
reputable sources mainly 
ONS and Statista Why we have chose the UK as our sustainable country:
• By living and studying in the UK, we are stakeholders in the UK 
energy system, allowing us to provide our own conceptual 
knowledge.
• The UK has a high availability of reliable data, from 
government sources (including ONS), and from Statista which 
is easily accessible to the public. 
• The energy price shocks of 2021-2023 have provided shock 
within the UK energy market and provide reason for policy 
change to help the welfare off the consumer.
• The UK government has stated a policy of which they have set 
targets for net zero in 2050, which enables us to build a report 
informing policy makers on progress and necessary changes 
to be made in order to achieve this goal.
Conceptual 
overview Theoretical foundations:
• Energy economics theory: In the short-run, domestic energy is typically 
price inelastic, and only becomes more elastic in the long-run. In the 
context of income-elasticity, energy tends to be income inelastic due to 
the majority of usage being used for heating which is a necessity for 
homes in the UK.
• Socio-demographic theory: Larger household size can result in a lower 
consumption per capita due to shared energy services. Overall UK 
population can drive overall aggregative consumption pointing it as a 
core macro-driver.
Conceptual foundation for multiple regression modelling:
• Isolates the marginal effect of each factor while controlling it for other 
inputs.
• Allows for model comparison and allows for testing effects of price 
changes.
• Supports ability for forecasting which allows to produce relevant 
recommendations for policymakers.

1. Executive Summary 
This report presents an analysis of the UK’s residential energy consumption to inform Government 
policy around the transition to sustainable energy. It addresses the issues around the 2050 Net 
Zero targets and the cost -of-living crisis, driven by over-reliance on imported gas. The objective 
is to analyse historical demand and forecast consumption from 2026 to 2030 informing 
government spending and focus. 
Using a top-down approach, we created multiple regression models analysing gas and electricity 
demand. Our findings show that gas demand is highly inelastic, constrained by the UK's older, 
less insulated housing stock. Alternatively, electricity demand is more elastic and positively linked 
to rising disposable income. The model shows cross -price sensitivity: when gas prices rise, 
electricity demand rises. However, the UK's marginal pricing mechanism links retail electricity to 
wholesale gas prices, financia lly punishing consumers and limiting the transition  to greener 
energy. 
To address these issues, this report recommends providing specific government grants to 
overcome high upfront costs for home insulation and heat pumps, implementing reforms to 
decouple electricity from gas prices, and increasing public education on efficient appliance use.  
 
2. Introduction  
2.1 Background & Client Context 
The United Kingdom's current energy landscape is characterised by issues between long-term 
environmental commitments and an ongoing cost-of-living crisis. While the nation has a mandate   
3 
to achieve Net Zero emissions by 2050 and agrees with the COP26 ambition of limiting global 
temperature increases to 1.5°C, UK households remain highly affected by extreme price volatility 
due to a reliance on imported international gas. 
Specifically, the domestic sector is responsible for around 26.8% of the UK's greenhouse gas 
emissions, largely because 64% of homes still rely on natural gas boilers for heating. Framed as 
an advisory analysis for policymakers, this report asserts that accurate energy demand modelling 
is imperative. Such data -driven modelling is required to guide infrastructure investments and 
implement policies that accelerate decarbonisation while actively managing the financial burden 
on homeowners. 
2.2 Rationale for Country Selection 
The United Kingdom was selected as the location for this study because of three primary factors. 
First, there is a high availability of publicly accessible economic data provided by institutions such 
as the Office for National Statistics  (ONS) and DESNZ. Secondly, the global gas price shocks 
experienced between 2021 and 2023 exposed problems within the UK energy system, showing 
there are deep rooted structural issues  within the country.  Finally, as residents and active 
stakeholders within the UK , we have  firsthand awareness of the socioeconomic impacts being 
modelled, helping provide context when interpreting data. 
2.3 Aims and Objectives 
This project aims to analyse and forecast UK residential energy consumption using  multiple 
regression models. The key objectives are to: 
● Identify key demographic, economic, and physical factors influencing domestic gas and 
electricity consumption. 
● Build a multiple linear regression model to analyse the impact of variables like household 
income and energy prices. 
● Calculate expected residential energy consumption trends over the next five-year period 
(2026–2030). 
● Deliver evidence-based policy recommendations to support the transition to sustainable 
energy and protect consumers from price shocks.

To maintain analytical focus, the system boundaries of this study are defined as: 
● In-Scope: A top-down analysis of UK residential gas and electricity consumption using

3. Literature Review  
3.1 Modelling Approaches (Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up) 
This report by Summerfield et al. (2009)  highlights the methodological differences between two 
modelling frameworks, ‘bottom -up’ and ‘top -down’. While ‘bottom -up’ modelling approaches 
attempt to capture physical processes of building stocks by incorporating variables regarding 
building characteristics, ‘top-down’ approaches focus on core macro -drivers such as GDP and 
population growth. As demonstrated by Summerfield et al. (2009) through their research models, 
using a ‘top-down’ approach allows for superior transparency and interpretability, through the use 
of comparative macro variables such as external temperature and GDP. A key benefit of a ‘top -
down’ approach is that models are based on actual consumption data, which is often easier to 
obtain and analyse, rather than theoretical building data, as seen in a ‘bottom -up’ model, which 
can be assumptive and difficult to obtain accurate data. Consequently, employing a ‘top -down’ 
approach provides a robust baseline tha t allows for research to take place and iden tify genuine 
consumption without being bounded by household variations. (Summerfield et al. 2009). 
 
3.2 Review of Marginal Pricing 
This publication by Pikk & Viiding (2014) explains that the UK's marginal pricing mechanism 
exposes the market to welfare detriments during global energy price shocks. It provides a 
foundational critique of the whole energy market design, which dissects the vulnerabilities 
associated with marginal  costing within the market. The idea of marginal pricing links the retail 
price of electricity to the extreme volatility of global commodity markets, disproportionately 
exposing the consumer to global price shocks,  even during periods where a large portion of the 
mix is made up of cheaper, renewable alternatives. Crucially, as the UK shifts towards a more 
renewable mix this pricing infrastructure becomes increasingly paradoxical, whereby there is 
more renewable energy produced, but is being charged to the market at the same price as more 
expensive gas production. Pikk & Viiding (2014) suggest that persisting with marginal costing in 
the long-run, as the system becomes more renewable dominant, will fail to provide any long-term 
price certainty which is required to incentivise capacity expansion, whilst failing to pass on 
economic benefits of a lower -carbon energy mix to the consumer. Consequently, any policy 
changes must consider decoupling electricity pricing from the  traditional marginal pricing model, 
in order for long -term success, decarbonisation and price -certainty for the consumer (Pikk & 
Viiding. 2014).  
   
5 
3.3 Elasticity & Welfare Shocks 
To enhance the predictive validity of a residential demand model, welfare and behavioural 
implications must be considered. Evidence from the report published by Levell, O’Connell & 
Smith. (2025)  suggests that there is an average price elasticity of 0.31 indicating that energy 
demand is inelastic, with only a small change in demand due to fluctuating costs of energy. This 
focuses on behavioural adjustments in relation to income, where the study es timates, with no 
government intervention, that the average household faces an overall welfare loss of 6% of after-
tax income, with the most vulnerable of households facing losses exceeding 11%. Notably, Levell, 
O’Connell & Smith. (2025 ) highlight how income alone is a poor indicator of these shocks, 
explaining only a small fraction of the variation in energy spending. For the UK energy 
consumption model, this necessitates the inclusion of variables beyond simple macroeconomic 
principles, such as housing efficiency which can be used to capture the heterogeneous nature of 
energy poverty. By integrating elasticity estimates, a proposed multiple regression model can be 
used to accurately simulate the trade -offs between price-driven demands and suppression, and 
the financial hardship that can threaten energy security. (Levell, O’Connell & Smith, 2025). 
 
3.4 Gas Reliance & Old Housing Stock 
The British energy market is characterised by a systematic vulnerability to external price shocks 
and long -run supply issues from global supply chain issues. According to the Energy Crisis 
Commission (2024), the UK is ‘dangerously underprepared’ for future energy crises largely due 
to high over-dependency on volatile worldwide gas wholesale markets and aging housing stock 
which is ranked amongst the least efficient in developed Europe. The findings stated by  the 
Energy Crisis Commission (2024)  suggest that energy efficiency and price elasticity are 
increasingly dominant factors in the context of the UK energy market. The article highlights the 
previously mentioned issues with the aging housing stock, leading to households being forced 
into a reactive consump tion cycle during periods of high cost, where consumers want to stay 
warm but are forced to cut heating during periods of high energy costs. This leads into the fact 
that any policy changes will have to be backed by an in -depth energy consumption model, an d 
must go beyond simple market -based pricing, in order to recommend any valid policy 
interventions. (UCL, Built Environment Faculty, 2024).

To move from the messy reality of the Rich Picture to a structured system of interest, the

● Customers: UK households (who benefit from stable prices) and policymakers (who

accurate, data-driven forecasts. 
● Weltanschauung / Worldview: The belief that proactive, data-driven planning is essential

● Owner: The UK Government / DESNZ, who own the ultimate policy goal of Net Zero.

Derived directly from this CATWOE analysis, the following root definition was created using the

"A system owned by the UK Government and operated by data analysts, to 
transform inaccurate, fragmented or incomplete estimates of residential 
energy demand into practical, comprehensive data -driven energy forecasts 
using multiple linear regression analysi s; in order to guide strategic policy 
interventions that protect UK households from price volatility while navigating

5. Methodology  
5.1 Data Collection & Sources 
To get a reliable picture of UK domestic energy usage our study took a top -down approach, 
analysing national trends using publicly available data to achieve our goal of forecasting UK 
domestic consumption as a whole to create actionable policy recommendati ons. We built a 
dataset covering 35 years, from 1990 to 2024, to ensure the accuracy of our forecast and its 
reliability in identifying meaningful trends. This data set was made up of data from the following 
sources: 
1. DESNZ - Overall consumption data and broken down into use case  (DESNZ, 2025a, 
2025b) 
2. ONS - Economic factors such as Median disposable income, GDP, Population, etc. (ONS, 
2025)  
3. Ofgem - Historical Gas and Electricity Prices (Ofgem, 2025) 
 
5.2 Analytical Approach 
We decided to use an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple linear regression model for this 
project to uncover the factors that hold the most weight on the UK’s domestic energy consumption, 
accurately forecast this consumption for the next 5 years and use this to provide data driven policy 
recommendations. We chose OLS because it can isolate the exact impact that movement in each 
individual factor can make on domestic consumption, this makes it the ideal tool to inform policy 
choices and predict policy outcomes across multiple scenarios. To further add to the usefulness 
of this model to the widest range of people, we had a large focus on making the output as intuitive 
as possible, ensuring all data was in its raw units (rather than converting to logarithms) allowing 
us to communicate our findings in real-world metrics such as gigawatt-hours rather than abstract 
percentages.

5.4 Model Specifications 
The selection process for what to be included in the model began with 15 potential 
macroeconomic and physical variables that we identified in part through the literature that we 
have previously discussed. A correlation analysis was done to filter out varia bles with weak 
relationships to energy consumption, from which 12 variables demonstrated strong correlations 
(above 0.8 or below -0.8). However, when running the regressions for gas and electricity with 
these 12 variables, clear signs of multicollinearity emerged in variables representing targeted use 
cases (e.g., natural gas for space heating, electricity for lighting) that were double counting the 
energy consumption data. This artificially inflated the model's explanatory power and impacted 
the accuracy of the coefficients. 
To resolve this the model was fine -tuned through a backward stepwise elimination approach, 
removing the weakest and most insignificant predictors one by one. This process continued until 
all remaining variables achieved statistical significance (a p-value 0.05). 
This left us with the same 5 variables for each model that proved to be statistically significant and 
were large drivers on the final consumption result. These were Electricity Price, Gas Price, the 
use of the other energy type (using gas use to predict electricity use, and vice versa), Median
