6. Findings 
6.1 Historical Trends / Context  
(Figure 6) 
Analysing the historical data spanning from 1990 to 2024 reveals the necessity for an inelastic 
nature of domestic energy consumption in the UK but also the severe volatility of the energy 
market due to factors outside of economic drivers such as geopoliti cs. Domestic energy 
consumption demonstrates a steady downward trend, driven by gradual efficiency improvements 
in appliances and rising baseline cost. However, we can see the impact geopolitical instability can 
have on domestic energy consumption between 2021 and 2023 where a surge in the energy price 
led to a large drop in consumption, exacerbated by the UK’s existing cost of living crisis. Despite 
these significant price shocks total domestic energy demand in the UK did not collapse 
proportionally, highl ighting that heating remains a fundamental inelastic necessity, largely 
because approximately 64% of UK households rely on aging gas boilers, leaving a vast majority 
of the population structurally vulnerable to the volatility of global wholesale gas markets. 
  
13 
6.2 Electricity Regression Output 
(Figure 7) 
The regression analysis for domestic electricity consumption had an Adjusted R -Square of 0.96 
meaning its variables can explain 96% of the variance in consumption. The output identified price 
as the primary mover of demand and allowed us to calculate that for every £1 per unit increase in 
electricity costs, domestic demand falls by approximately 100 Gigawatt-hours, an amount roughly 
equivalent to the annual consumption of 37,000 homes. Through digging into this further the 
model uncovered a substitution effect between the two energy commodities; a £1 increase in gas 
prices results in a rise of 233 Gigawatt-hours (equivalent to 81,000 homes) in electricity demand. 
This indicates that as gas becomes unaffordable, consumers actively shift their consumption 
behaviours toward secondary electrical sources, such as plug-in space heaters.

0.96 meaning its variables can explain 96% of the variance in consumption. From this model we 
found a clear "Wealth Effect", through median disposable income having a negative coefficient 
which suggests that as UK households grow wealthier, they naturally tend to move away from the 
consumption of gas toward modern, electric alternatives. However, the regression also highlights 
a risk towards decarbonization targets: the interaction between the prices of Gas and Electricity 
on each other’s consumption means high electricity prices can inadvertently drive consumers 
back toward established gas infrastructure despite the willingness to reduce gas consumption. 
Therefore, i f electricity remains too expensive, households are financially disincentivised from 
adopting heat pumps, which threatens to stall the national Net Zero agenda. 
6.4 5-Year Forecast (2025-2030) 
We used the above-mentioned regression models to forecast energy demand from 2024 to 2029 
for Electricity and Gas under two primary scenarios. 
 
● Scenario 1 (Status Quo):  Without policy intervention and assuming electricity prices 
continue to increase the model predicts that heavy reliance on gas will persist. In this 
scenario the forecast predicts a 10% decrease in gas consumption and an 11% decrease 
in electricity consum ption between 2024 and 2029. The decline in consumption across 
electricity and gas reflects the shrinking of energy demand as due to economic factors 
such as the cost -of-living crisis, rather than a successful green transition as co nsumers 
are forced to use less energy overall to make ends meet. The UK population lacks the 
disposable income required to overcome the "green premium"  associated with 
transitioning to sustainable infrastructure like heat pumps or electric vehicles. 
(Figure 9) 
● Scenario 2 (Policy Shift): However, if targeted policy changes get electricity prices back 
down to pre -Covid levels and the government proactively subsidises necessary 
  
15 
infrastructure (such as EV charging networks and residential heat pump grants), the 
forecast predicts a dramatic consumption shift. In this scenario, the forecast shows a 51% 
reduction in gas consumption with a 20% increase in electricity consumption by 20 29, 
showing what a market-driven approach to reduce our reliance on fossil fuels could look 
like. As electricity becomes the more economical energy source households will actively 
substitute gas for electricity, acting as a cheaper and safer option as the UK consumer is 
less impacted by future geopolitical gas price shocks. 
(Figure 10) 
7. Discussion 
7.1 Interpretation of Results  
The regression model highlights a distinct divergence in domestic energy trends. Electricity 
demand shows a positive correlation with median disposable income: as consumers grow 
wealthier, increased acquisition of electronics and modern appliances is inherently associated 
with higher baseline electricity usage. 
Conversely, gas consumption operates primarily as a highly inelastic physical necessity. This is 
tied to the UK's ageing, poorly insulated housing stock, which requires a high level of British 
Thermal Units (BTUs) to maintain comfortable temperatures, leaving households reliant on 
burning gas regardless of price. However, a negative coefficient for disposable income regarding 
gas consumption implies that wealthier populations natural ly make the transition away from gas 
reliance, an association likely linked  to investments in retrofitting, insulation, or electric heat 
pumps. 
Crucially, the model reveals a cross-price sensitivity: for every £1 increase in gas prices, electricity 
demand rises by approximately 233 Gigawatt-hours. This substitution effect suggests households 
  
16 
resort to electric plug-in heaters when central gas heating becomes unaffordable. Within the UK's 
marginal pricing mechanism, where wholesale electricity is often pegged to expensive gas 
generation, global gas volatility strongly correlates with inflated e lectricity bills. If these inflated 
electricity prices persist, they risk stalling decarbonisation by removing the financial incentive to 
abandon established gas infrastructure. 
To investigate this substitution effect, the model intentionally included the opposing energy type's 
total consumption as an independent variable. This choice tries to capture interconnected 
household behaviours, such as replacing gas central heating with supplementary electrical 
heating, that broad price indices might miss, albeit introducing some statistical constraints. 
 
7.2 Comparison with Existing Literature  
The model’s indication of highly inelastic gas consumption aligns strongly with the findings of the 
Energy Crisis Commission (UCL, Built Environment Faculty, 2024) , which characterises the UK 
as highly vulnerable due to its ageing, inefficient housing stock. This structural inefficiency traps 
households in what the literature describes as a "reactive consumption cycle." This agrees with 
our model's finding that gas usage is strongly linked to physical necessity and thermal constraints 
rather than purely choice. Furthermore, the inelastic nature of this demand is supported by Levell, 
O’Connell, and Smith (2025), who estimate an average price elasticity of just 0.31. Our model’s 
outputs agree with their assertion that such inelasticity exposes households to severe welfare 
losses during price shocks, as consumers cannot easily reduce their baseline heating 
requirements. 
Regarding socio-demographic factors, the finding that electricity demand rises with disposable 
income adds nuance to the assertions of Levell, O’Connell, and Smith (2025).  They note that 
income alone is often a poor predictor of total energy spending variation. Our model clarifies this 
dynamic by disaggregating the fuels: wealth shows a positive association with baseline electricity 
consumption, likely via lifestyle choices and appliance adoption, but does not inherently correlate 
with gas consumption, highlighting the heterogeneous nature of domestic energy poverty. 
Crucially, the model’s observed cross -price sensitivity, where electricity demand rises alongside 
gas prices, illustrates the vulnerabilities of the UK's marginal pricing mechanism outlined by Pikk 
and Viiding (2014).  By linking retail electricity to volatile global commodity markets, the current 
system disproportionately exposes consumers to external shocks. Our analysis indicates that 
without the pricing decoupling recommended by Pikk and Viiding, the economic benefi ts of a 
renewable energy transition may  fail to reach consumers, potentially stalling broader 
decarbonisation efforts. 
Finally, the successful identification of these macroeconomic trends helps validate the 
methodological framework endorsed by Summerfield et al. (2009).  The top -down approach 
provided a strong, baseline of aggregate consumption, avoiding the complexities associated with 
bottom-up models and information.   
17 
 
7.3 Implementation Awareness & Project Adaptation 
During the progression of this study, several methodological and data -related challenges 
emerged that required changes. Firstly, the identification of multicollinearity during the initial 
modelling phase. When incorporating specific consumption variables alongside broader 
economic indicators, the model exhibited overlapping patterns, which threatened the reliability of 
the outputs. To resolve this and ensure statistical robustness, we iteratively adapted the model, 
filtering the dataset down from over 16 initial factors to the 5 most statistically significant variables. 
Furthermore, sourcing consistent, long -term historical data for specific independent variables 
presented a distinct challenge. For instance, where long -term household price data was 
fragmented or unavailable, we had to adapt by calculating implied prices to ensure the regression 
analysis could proceed. While this data engineering allowed for the creation of a functional model, 
it introduces a reliance on manually calculated inputs. Navigating these constraints was essential 
to maintaining the structural integrity of the baseline 5-year forecast. 
 
8. Assumptions & Limitations 
8.1 Methodological Limitations 
Firstly, one limitation of this study is the exclusion of Heating Degree Days (HDD). By relying on 
average temperature, the model assumes a relatively flat weather baseline, failing to capture the 
extreme winter demand peaks that can stress the energy grid and household finances. 
Furthermore, the top-down approach introduces aggregation bias. By utilising national-level data, 
the model cannot account for small scale variations or the impact of local competition, such as 
disruptive energy providers altering localised consumer behaviour. This reliance on macro -data 
also risks omitted variabl e’s including  relevant qualitative factors, (like pro-environmental 
attitudes) which are unquantifiable and therefore excluded. Additionally, reporting discrepancies 
between rural and urban areas may subtly skew the national averages. 
Another limitation of the regression specifications is the inclusion of gas consumption as a 
predictor in the electricity model, and vice versa. While it was intended to capture behavioural 
substitution, both variables are fundamentally driven by the exact same factors (e.g., temperature, 
income, and housing inefficiency). Consequently, the analysis captures shared seasonal and 
economic patterns rather than the isolated effect of one fuel upon the other. This mean s the 
exceptionally high Adjusted R -Squared values (approx. 0.96) could be artificially inflated by this 
shared variance.   
18 
Finally, OLS regression modelling is inherently linear. Real-world energy transitions, such as the 
mass adoption of heat pumps or the effects of policy interventions, frequently exhibit non -linear 
trajectories. The model's structural simplicity may therefore struggle to precisely project the long-
term impacts of green infrastructure integration. 
 
8.2 Data Limitations 
A notable limitation regarding data integrity stems from the necessity to manually calculate certain 
regression inputs, such as historical energy prices. While the analysis evaluates 35 years of 
historical data, calculating implied prices rather than utilising explicit, pre-existing datasets 
inherently introduces potential error into the model's foundation. 
Additionally, the historical datasets contain a significant weakness due to the COVID -19 
pandemic. The sudden transition to working from home in 2020 fundamentally changed domestic 
consumption patterns across the UK. This widespread behavioural shift introduces major volatility 
into the historical trendline, which may distort the baseline averages used in future projections. 
Finally, the purely top-down approach restricts the model's ability to analyse the effects of small-
scale changes. Sudden technological or regulatory shifts, such as the phased introduction of LED 
lighting standards, create household-level efficiency gains that are difficult to isolate or explicitly 
account for within utilising national data. 
 
8.3 Forecasting Assumptions 
The projections for the 2026-2030 period rely on the assumption that historical trends will continue 
without major external shocks. For instance, to generate the baseline forecast, the model 
assumes that variables such as median disposable income and population will grow linearly 
based on historical averages. In a volatile global economy, these linear assumptions may not hold 
true. 
Crucially, the alternate forecast scenario, which models a decrease in electricity prices causing a 
shift away from gas, assumes a successful decoupling of electricity prices from gas prices. It is 
important to acknowledge that altering this marginal pricing mechanism is a highly complex 
political challenge, not merely an economic model adjustment. Many governments have 
attempted market reforms without long-term success, making this a significant real -world barrier 
to realising the forecasted demand shifts.  
Furthermore, any projected transition away from gas assumes that the required physical 
infrastructure, such as localised grid capacity and EV charging’s, will be deployed rapidly enough 
to meet rising electricity demand. If policy or infrastructure development lags, these forecasts will 
likely incorrectly estimate the speed of residential decarbonisation. 
   
19 
9. Conclusion, Recommendations, and Further 
Steps 
9.1 Conclusion 
This project has successfully delivered a robust multiple linear regression model and a five -year 
baseline forecast to evaluate the primary drivers of UK residential energy consumption. The 
analysis reveals a fundamental divergence in domestic energy use. Specifically, gas demand 
remains highly inelastic and is heavily constrained by the physical realities of an ageing housing 
stock, whereas electricity demand demonstrates greater elasticity and a positive correlation with 
growing disposable income. Crucial ly, the model highlights a major vulnerability stemming from 
the UK's marginal pricing mechanism. By pegging retail electricity to wholesale gas markets, the 
current framework creates a situation where high gas prices inadvertently inflate electricity costs. 
This dynamic financially penalises consumers and actively risks stalling the broader transition to 
Net Zero, demonstrating the urgent need for targeted, data-driven policy interventions. 
 
9.2 Recommendations for Policymakers 
The UK residential energy market is highly vulnerable to global price volatility due to its structural 
dependence on gas. Because marginal pricing ties the electricity price to the most expensive 
method of production, this can lessen the reduced pricing effects of renewable generation. As the 
amount of renewable generation increases, this can help to reduce the magnitude and frequency 
of price spikes. If energy prices were to return to pre -2021 levels, as assumed in Scenario 2 of 
our forecast, and the growth of renewable energy production continues at an expanding rate, it is 
feasible for renewables to consistently supply over 50% of the energy supply by 2029. In turn, 
this means the removal of marginal pricing can be looked at as a long-term reform as renewables 
continue to be an increasing part of the mix. 
 
Efficiency improvements are another recommendation for reducing consumption and mitigating 
system stress. Interventions such as insulation upgrades, heat -pump instalment and improved 
efficiency of boilers will together combine to create a more efficient energy system. As noted in 
the findings, as electricity prices decrease this will encourage more households to switch their 
heating methods from gas to electric, therefore  increasing efficiency and saving on bills. These 
effects should be focused on older, poorly insulated  homes, often with low -income residents, 
however policy intervention is required to provide upfront investment for household changes. 
 
Behavioural change forms the third key recommendation for reducing overall consumption and 
supporting a more resilient heating system. Adjustments in education such as improved 
management of heating schedules, reductions in hot water usage and wastage, and more efficient 
operations of household appliances, each contribute small reductions in demand, but when 
combined on a national level, the cumulative effect becomes significant, easing pressure on the   
20 
system during periods of high demand. Within the policy shift forecasting scenario, it is evident 
that all efficiency improvements are vital to prevent unnecessary energy growth, if  small 
behavioural changes reduced demand by 3 -5% this would offset some of the electricity growth, 
therefore allowing renewables to cover a larger share of overall consumption. 
 
9.3 Further Steps for the Model 
Future iterations of this residential energy model must incorporate a specific climate variable, 
such as Heating Degree Days (HDD). Relying solely on average temperatures limits the model's 
ability to account for severe seasonal demand volatility.  
Furthermore, as the UK increases its renewable infrastructure to decrease reliance on gas, future 
models must also account for the weather-dependent nature of wind and solar generation on the 
supply side.  
Transitioning from a purely top -down approach to a hybrid framework would also significantly 
enhance forecasting accuracy. By integrating bottom-up data, such as the National Grid's Future 
Energy Scenarios (FES), the model could better account for other limitations like the adoption 
rates of electric vehicles and residential heat pumps.  
In addition, because gas and electricity demand influence each other simultaneously, future 
models should make use of advanced statistical techniques (Vector Autoregression) to separate 
the overlapping relationship, resulting in a more accurate and reliable baseline forecast. 
Finally, introducing regional changes are recommended to investigate how geographic 
temperature differences and regional income divides affect localised energy usage.

1. Background and Context 
The group provides a clear overview of InnoWave Global and effectively identifies knowledge 
fragmentation and coordination breakdowns as key organisational challenges. The Innovation 
Strategist persona is well developed and helps humanise the problem, illustrating how duplicated 
work, limited visibility across regions, and administrative overload affect day-to-day practice. 
However, the background analysis could be strengthened by deeper engagement with 
organisational and industry context, particularly in explaining why these challenges are 
especially acute for InnoWave rather than common to all large consultancies. 
2. Problem Statement 
The problem is framed coherently around inefficiency, fragmentation, and lost innovation 
capacity, and the narrative around “administrative nightmares” makes the issues accessible. That 
said, the problem definition remains quite broad and occasionally blends into solution language, 
which weakens analytical sharpness. More explicit prioritisation of which pain points matter 
most—and how they manifest at specific moments in the workflow—would help clarify the core 
problem the solution is designed to address. 
3. Solution and Features 
WaveAssist and InnoBot are presented as an integrated, enterprise-wide augmentation solution 
with a strong emphasis on collaboration and knowledge access. The report makes a clear effort to 
differentiate the system from rule-based tools through semantic search and group-based AI 
interaction. However, despite this clarification, the explanation of how the AI actually reasons, 
learns, or adapts remains limited. Several features are described in conceptual or aspirational 
terms, making it difficult to fully assess what is technically novel versus what relies on improved 
interface and integration. Greater clarity on AI mechanisms and boundaries would strengthen the 
solution’s credibility. 
4. Project Management, Presentation, and Report 
The report is clearly organised and transparently structured around the presentation slides,

Or in other words, no text in the assignment can be written by any AI tool.  In today’s workplaces, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly introduced to augment workers’ capabilities. This individual assignment asks you to critically examine the socio-technical dimensions of AI adoption in such contexts and to explore how organizations can manage digital transformation when work is enhanced by AI.   The goal is to assess your ability to engage deeply with course concepts and scholarly literature on digital transformation, AI and socio-technical systems, while structuring a clear and coherent argument.  In your essay, you should address the following questions:  • AI’s Unique Features & Strategic Value: Describe the unique features of modern AI (e.g. machine learning, generative AI, data-driven decision support) that distinguish it from earlier workplace technologies. Explain how these features enable the augmentation of knowledge work and creative tasks, providing examples of how AI-human collaboration can drive strategic value or innovation in organizations.  • First-Order and Second-Order Effects: Examine the immediate impacts (first-order effects) of introducing AI augmentation on workflows, employee roles, and productivity, as well as the longer-term or emergent consequences (second-order effects) on organizational structure and social dynamics. Consider how augmented AI tools might disrupt established formal structures or the informal “social fabric” of the workplace. For example, does AI augmentation change how teams collaborate or make decisions? Does it redistribute expertise and alter power dynamics?  • Managing the Adoption of AI Augmentation: Given these socio-technical effects, discuss how organizations should manage the adoption process of AI-augmented work. What strategies can ensure that human–AI collaboration is successful and sustainable? In your discussion, consider the role of leadership and the HR function in change management: for instance, training employees to work effectively with AI, redesigning jobs to balance human and AI strengths, addressing employee concerns (like trust in AI or fear of change), and establishing

These are not an exhaustive list, but they offer useful insights and frameworks that you may find relevant: - Fuegener et al. (2021, MIS Quarterly): “Will Humans-in-the-Loop Become Borgs? Merits and Pitfalls of Working with AI.” – A multi-method study on human–AI decision-making, finding that while AI advice can improve individual task accuracy, it may also cause workers’ decisions to converge and reduce unique human knowledge - Abdel-Karim et al. (2022, MIS Quarterly): “How AI-Based Systems Can Induce Reflections: The Case of AI-Augmented Diagnostic Work.” – An empirical study of doctors using an AI decision support tool. - Anthony et al. (2023, Organization Science): “‘Collaborating’ with AI: Taking a System View to Explore the Future of Work.” – A conceptual article that applies socio-technical and organizational theory to AI. It argues that we should view AI not just as a tool, but as a counterpart in a work system, and calls for studying how AI’s design, implementation and use are intertwined with work practices. - Raisch & Krakowski (2021, Academy of Management Review): “Artificial Intelligence and Management: The Automation–Augmentation Paradox.” – A theoretical piece discussing the intertwined nature of AI automation and augmentation. It posits that augmentation (AI complementing humans) cannot be neatly separated from automation; over-emphasizing one side can create paradoxical tensions and unintended consequences. - Jia et al. (2024, Academy of Management Journal): “When and How Artificial Intelligence Augments Employee Creativity.” – A mixed-method field study (including an experiment in a company) examining AI assistance in a sales task. It found that AI can boost employees’ creative performance (by taking over routine parts of work so humans focus on complex tasks), but the benefits were “skill-biased,” favoring experts over less-skilled workers. - Shao et al. (2024, Journal of Management): “Using Augmentation-Based AI Tool at Work: A Daily Investigation of Learning-Based Benefit and Challenge.” – A diary study of employees’ daily interactions with an AI tool. It highlights a dual effect: frequent use of an AI assistant led to knowledge gains and better performance, yet also caused information overload that impaired recovery and performance by day’s end. Company Background: InnoWave Global 
InnoWave Global  is a multinational professional services and technology company with 
approximately 25,000 employees spread across Europe, Asia and North America. 
Headquartered in London, the company provides a mix of consulting, digital transformation 
services and techno logy-enabled solutions for clients in industries ranging from healthcare 
and finance to retail and consumer goods. 
The company grew rapidly over the last decade through acquisitions of boutique 
consultancies and technology providers. While this expansion has allowed InnoWave to 
diversify its expertise and client base, it has also created challenges: regional offices of ten 
operate with their own processes and digital tools, making it difficult to share knowledge and 
collaborate across the global network. Employees have voiced frustration about duplicated 
work, inconsistent systems and limited opportunities to experiment with new ways of 
working. 
The competitive environment has also intensified. On one side, agile start-ups are introducing 
AI-driven platforms and services at a much faster pace, threatening to disrupt traditional 
consulting offerings. On the other, large global firms  with deeper resources are building 
innovation ecosystems and heavily investing in AI -powered employee augmentation. 
InnoWave is therefore squeezed between nimble disruptors and powerful incumbents. 
Despite these pressures, InnoWave has maintained strong client relationships, thanks to its 
reputation for blending analytical expertise with creative problem -solving. Many of its 
flagship projects involve working closely with clients to design new digital services, improve 
customer experiences or create innovative strategies for entering new markets. Success 
depends on the ability of employees to bring both technical knowledge and creativity to how 
they work and develop solutions for their clients. 
Recognising the urgency of change, the Board of Directors has announced a new Digital 
Innovation and Transformation Programme . The vision is not to automate work or reduce 
headcount but to augment employees with AI — empowering them to work more creatively, 
make faster and better -informed decisions and collaborate seamlessly across regions. The 
ambition is to create a more connected, knowledge -driven organisation that attracts top 
talent, inspires innovation and gai ns a sustainable competitive edge in a rap idly evolving 
marketplace. 
Roles to choose from. Your consulting team must select one role of the following three roles 
within InnoWave Global as the focus of your project: 
1. Business Analyst 
Business Analysts support client projects by gathering data from multiple sources, 
synthesising trends, and producing reports, models and visualisations that inform decision -
making. They work closely with consultants and client teams to ensure findings are aligned 
with business objectives. The role demands strong quantitative reasoning, attention to detail 
and the ability to communicate complex results in accessible ways.

Files/Year 4/Philosophy of Mind/Behaviou:
Can the behaviourist provide a convincing account of how we 
can know other people’s mental states? What about our own? 
 
 
Rylean, or philosophical, behaviourism, is a theory that rejects the Cartesian picture of the mind 
as an inner, private object separate from the body. It instead defines the mind and mental states 
in terms of patterns of behaviour, and dispositions to behave in various circumstances. It comes 
as a direct rebuttal to Cartesian dualism, as he calls Descartes’ definition of the mind - and the 
separation of the mind and body into two different ‘substances’  (Descartes, 1641/1984) - a 
‘category mistake’ (Ryle, 1949). Ryle argues that treating the mind as an inner, ‘ghost -like’ 
object is a fundamental error in classification, and that mental concepts, such as beliefs, desires 
and intentions, should lie in a different logical category. According to Ryle, these terms do not 
refer to occult, inner states of the mind hidden from third parties; he says that to ‘believe’ that 
Paris is in France, is simply to be disposed to answer questions, navigate maps, and act in ways 
showing that belief. The appeal of this view is that i t solves the problem of knowing ‘other 
minds’ by making the mind a public entity by definition. If the mind is identical to observable 
behaviour, nothing is private or inner- we can know another mind’s state just by watching it. 
In a crude form, this seems to imply that if a person got stabbed, they would only become ‘in 
pain’ the moment they started screaming, said the words ‘I am in pain’ or otherwise manifested 
the relevant dispositions- until that moment there would be no pain, only bodily damage. This 
sounds highly implausible- naturally we know they will experience the qualitative feeling of 
being in pain from the moment of injury, whether they manifest it or not. Such cases suggest 
that mental states should not be identified purely with overt behaviour, and that behaviourism 
risks leaving out the experiential aspect of mental states altogether. 
Even leaving qualia aside, behaviourism seems unable to provide a complete account of how 
we can know other people’s mental states for some very simple reasons, such as the fact that 
people tend to think one way and act another surprisingly often. Behavioural economics theory 
outlines the difference between ‘stated preferences’, which are what we say we prefer; and 
‘revealed preferences’, which are inferred from our choices  (Samuelson, 1938). We are prone 
to showing behaviour that directly conflicts with our true mental states, whether we are 
intentionally acting or being deceptive, or simply do not have good enough self-awareness. We 
can, for example, subconsciously conform to social pressur es in a social situation and 
unintentionally agree with a controversial statement we wouldn’t actually agree with privately 
upon reflection. A strict behaviourist would observe our accidental agreement, take it for face 
value, and ascribe us to the belief expressed in the remark- therefore inaccurately understanding 
our true beliefs. 
Behaviours can also be misinterpreted - the behaviourist holds the responsibility to interpret 
their observations correctly. The Geach-Chisholm (1957) objection states that it is 
inappropriate to map a behaviour such as running away from a snake, to exclusively one 
corresponding mental state such a phobia of snakes, since reality is much more complex.  Whether an ophidiophobic person runs away from a snake depends not only on their disposition 
of fear, but also a network of further beliefs and desires simultaneously, such as a belief that 
the snake is dangerous, a belief that running away is a viable esc ape method, or even a desire 
to survive. Conversely, even someone who does recognise the danger of the snake and realises 
they can safely escape, might not in fact run away if they lack a desire to preserve their life. A 
behaviourist may observe an ophidiophobe approaching this snake, without the knowledge that 
they are suicidal, and wrongly conclude that they are not afraid of snakes. 
 
Radical behaviourism, developed by B.F. Skinner  (1977), takes a more scientific, 
psychological approach to the link between the mind and behaviour than Ryle’s philosophical 
behaviourism. Despite fundamental differences, their commonalities make them a relevant 
comparison. Both views downplay or reject appeali ng to inner, unobservable mental states as 
explanatory causes for behaviour, instead focusing only on what can be observed. While Ryle 
provides conceptual analysis of mental states in terms of actions and dispositions, Skinner, and 
other experimental behav iourists such as Ivan Pavlov  (1927), scientifically investigated how 
behaviour is shaped by environmental factors. Their studies on operant and classical 
conditioning suggest that behavioural patterns are learnt and can be explained by 
environmental reinforcement, without giving credit to i nner mental objects. These theories fit 
well with Ryle’s emphasis on observable behaviour and provide empirical grounding for the 
behavioural patterns Ryle talks about.  
However, both philosophical and psychological behaviourism face a similar epistemic 
limitation. All we can do is observe the behaviour, even if predictably, and then provide some 
theory for why it happens. They may offer useful, or even valid, explanations of behaviour, but 
they do not give us any insight into what the subject is really thinking or experiencing. It is not 
impossible that Pavlov’s dog had an intentional thought process of “watch what I can make 
Pavlov do. As soon as I drool, he’ll smile and write in his little book ” (Stivers, 2003), rather 
than merely undergoing the automatic process of operant conditioning. Although it is extremely 
unlikely for a dog to actually think this way, the joke makes a serious point that we are also 
similarly susceptible to conditioning and this sort of intentional deception is very possible with 
humans. Both kinds of behaviourism provide, at best, a seemingly logical story that links 
observed bodily manifestations to hypothetical inner processes. They do not reveal the private 
intentions of the mind committing the act; we still do not know what is happening ‘behind the 
curtain’. 
The behaviourist may counter that the ‘mind’ is actually what is in front of the curtain, rather 
than behind. However, this claim seems to disagree with our general, established understanding 
of the term. Standard dictionary definitions of the word ‘mind’ typically refer to the ‘ghost -
like’ phenomena such as thought, feelings, consciousness and experience, all of which we 
naturally locate behind the curtain of our skin, and in the brain. This suggests that not only does 
behaviourism attempt to describe the mind, but is proposing a fundamental revision of our 
common conception of it in which mental states are identified with and defined by our outward 
behaviour or disposition. If our widely accepted understanding of the mind refers to inner 
aspects of our lives, then a theory that focuses exclusively on the outer, observable, behavioural  parts is unlikely to provide a complete account of another person’s true mental state, especially 
if it relies on behaviourism alone. 
 
Behaviourism rightly emphasises that there is a close connection between mental states and 
behaviour. For the average person, it is extremely difficult to be in severe pain without 
manifesting it in any observable way. It is therefore natural to treat someone’s behaviour as an 
at least partially reliable indicator of what they may be thinking or feeling.  
The ‘Super-Spartan’ thought experiment presents a subject who trains himself to never display 
any reaction to pain. Taking this even further, we can consider a subject who aims to become a 
‘perfect stoic’. He trains to eliminate not only reactions to pain, but any outward sign that might 
reveal his mental state, practically exhibiting no observable behaviour at all. 
However, even this impossibly extreme example, can be re -described by the behaviourist 
simply as a pattern of ‘stoic behaviour', manifesting his inner mental state of desire to become 
stoic. The very attempt to conceal his mental state becomes evidence of those states, because 
it is impossible to ‘not behave’. The fact that even a lack of behaviour does not refute 
behaviourism- which relies on behaviour- makes behaviourism seem potentially unfalsifiable 
and thin due to its elasticity. This example makes it unclear whether the mental state has been 
actually explained, or just re-labelled. 
 
Ultimately, behaviourism at least provides a starting point for knowing others’ mental states. 
We all are behaving in some way whether we want to or not, and our behaviours reflect some 
reason or cause whether we are conscious of them or not. Of course, it is easier to infer the 
reason or cause with our most basic and instinctual mental states- if someone is screaming and 
bleeding, they are probably in pain, and if they are eating, they probably feel hungry. However, 
minds have the propensity to obscure their more complex behaviours, intentionally or not, 
producing behaviour that diverges from their true beliefs, desires or feelings. Without doing 
additional detective work, it is difficult to identify this obscurity, therefore we shouldn’t judge 
people’s mental states solely using the behaviourist method. In practice, our judgements about 
others’ mental states also rely on other things such as contextual information, knowledge of the 
person, their own testimony, as well as our own capacity to imagine what it would be like to 
be that person. 
 
To assess the ability of the behaviourist to provide an account of our own minds, we must 
address the asymmetry between self-knowledge, and knowledge of others. I may know others’ 
mental states primarily through observation, whereas I appear to know and experience my own 
mind directly from the inside. For Ryle, however, self -knowledge is not a matter of peering 
into a private realm, but of knowing how I am disposed to behave in various circumstances- to 
know that I am in pain, is essentially to know how I a m disposed to react and respond when I 
am hurt.   This picture seems to get self -knowledge the wrong way around. If ‘pain’ was identical to a 
pattern of ‘pain behaviour’, then I would need to first observe my own behaviour to know that 
I am in pain. Yet, I can know that I am in pain before the moment I wince or state the words ‘I 
am in pain’ (which would let others know that I am in pain at that moment), even if I 
successfully suppress any such outward signs. I have ‘privileged access’ to my own mind, and 
I have the ability of introspection unmediated by observation of my behaviour. 
However, our introspective abilities and privileged access are not infallible. We do not have 
perfect ‘incorrigible’ access to our own minds as Descartes envisaged. Contemporary 
philosophy and psychology suggest that our minds are vulnerable to subconscious processes, 
biases and introspective ‘illusions’ which may distort how we understand ourselves. 
Nevertheless, the knowledge we have of ourselves is far wider than even of our closest friends 
or family members, simply because we have continuous access to our mental lives in a way 
that others do not. 
Importantly, we have exclusive access to our own qualitative experiences. Even a parent who 
has known me my whole life, and knows everything there is to know about me, cannot literally 
experience what ‘it is like’ to be me. This asymmetry in access to qualia reinforces the idea that 
the behavioural resources offered by behaviourism alone, are not enough for a plausible 
account of self-knowledge. 
 
As mentioned earlier, the ability to imagine or simulate what it would be like to be another 
person is crucial in forming an idea of their mental state. This capacity can otherwise be 
described as empathy, and it stands to our knowledge of other minds, muc h like how self -
awareness stands to our knowledge of our own. Both are fallible yet learnable skills which, 
when combined with observation of behaviour, form a much richer account of mental states 
than behaviourism alone. Thought experiments such as Thomas Nagel’s ‘What is it like to be a 
bat?’ (1974) and Frank Jackson’s ‘Mary’ s Room’ (1986) highlight both the power and the 
limitations of this imaginative route. 
In both cases, we are asked to imagine being in a mental state different from our current one, 
while possessing complete theoretical knowledge about that mind. In Nagel’s case, we imagine 
the mind of a completely different being to us - a bat. We know every thing there is to know 
about bats’ behaviour - flying around, not being able to see, making clicking sounds and 
noticing how long it takes for the echo of that click to return to you, sleeping upside down, et 
cetera. In Jackson’s case, for argument’s sake we can imagine that Mary is us and that we know 
all the physical and behavioural facts about colour vision, but have never seen the colour red 
and must imagine what it would be like to see it for the first time. In both cases, there seems to 
be a certain kind of knowledge missing just beyond our grasp, even if we are Mary and are 
essentially just introspecting into a variation of our own minds where we have never seen the 
colour red. When Mary sees red for the first time, it would be natural to say that she does learn 
something new, despite her previous, apparently exhaustive, knowledge. There is a contrast 
between the third -person knowledge, and the first -person experiential qu alia which are 
crucially missing from the pure behaviourist view.   
Ultimately, we can never perfectly know or imagine the state of another mind, especially 
judging solely off the behaviour of the body attached to that mind. Actions and dispositions are 
a great starting source of evidence, since there is always a reason fo r everything we do, even 
when we are not fully aware of it. However given our human proneness to deceive and act, 
intentionally or not, outward behaviour should not always be fully relied on. Sometimes we 
need other sources of evidence of the mind state, such as contextual knowledge, empathising, 
or simply asking the person to share their inner introspective insights with you. The more we 
learn about a person’s behavioural patterns of action and reaction, the better equipped we are 
to understand their mental state. Although, this understanding relies on methods outside of the 
behaviourist’s reach. To ignore empathy, and to judge a bat or fellow human solely by what 
they do and how they act, is shallow and limits greatly our ability to know others’ minds.  
We may never know, or more specifically feel, 'what it is like to be a bat', but we can surely get 
a pretty good idea with enough knowledge and imagination. It may be easier to approximate 
other human’s experiences more closely than a bat’s since we share a more similar form of life 
and can relate to each other better.  
As for our own minds, we are already currently knowing our own minds to a certain extent- we 
are continuously experiencing our feelings, whether we choose to act on them, or observe them, 
or not. Our introspection is not infallible - we may have personal bi ases that sometimes make 
us view others through a more accurate lens than ourselves, but ultimately, we know and feel 
things about ourselves no behaviourist could ever learn through observation.

Topic of Study
This report will investigate the ethical dynamic 
between xAI and the companies’ founder and CEO, 
Elon Musk. The speciﬁc focus will be on the blurred 
boundary between personal founder ideology and 
corporate ethical positioning. The study will ‘zoom in’ 
on how wrapping up personal ethics with a ﬁrm 
collapses the traditional separation of ownership 
and control- and how this governance structure 
allows the founder’s ethical compass to fundamentally 
dictate product output (e.g. content moderation 
guidelines on X, Grok AI parameters).
Founder-Firm Integration Rationale (Why This Matters)
This topic has ripple effects that spread across 
to many facets of society, and its’ impacts are 
signiﬁcant in the current socio-economic 
environment. As AI systems become central to 
the global ﬂow of information, ethical guardrails 
will become under heavier scrutiny, and the 
regulatory environment will also respond. What 
are the consequences of the actions of a 
company who’s ethical accountability is very 
closely tied with a single individual’s ideology?

this report will triangulate

public social media statements regarding 
absolute free speech.
 Framework 1: Agency Theory + 
Corporate Governance³
Musk is both the principal and the agent of xAI; introducing the Agency Theory problem. Because 
CEOs may act on their own agendas instead of the company’s best interest, Corporate Governance 
(like a Board of Directors) exists to monitor them and keep them ethical. This case is an example of how 
bypassing such guidelines can create a shortcut in the corporate governance pipeline, where a single 
person’s ideology can immediately become the ethical output of a product used by billions globally. 
This framework will be used to measure the extent of this consequence.
 Framework 2: 
‘Stakeholder 
Salience’ Model⁴
This model will be used to analyse and map Musk’s 
own stakeholder status- as well as to categorise 
how xAI prioritises different groups of 
stakeholders, and subsequent responsiveness to 
their demands. The model will help investigate the 
concentration of power within the ﬁrm, by 
applying it across members at the top of the 
organisational hierarchy, and comparing the 
salience of the most ‘powerful’ and ‘legitimate’ 
stakeholders of the company.

Coursework Assignment 2025-6  
ACF318: Professional Ethics  
Department of Accounting and Finance, Lancaster University  
 
Additional Guidance  
(to be read alongside the module outline) 
 
This coursework assignment asks each student to undertake a detailed ethical review of a single 
organisation of their own choice.  The goal of the review is to provide something that a student 
might be able to present to an ethically aware investor, new senior employee, or other stakeholder 
in the business who wants a better understanding of how ethics forms a part of organisational 
activity, decision making, the social and environment context within which it exists, or any other 
area where ethics has an impact, or should have an impact.  
 
The report should not be addressed to the organisation, it should not be written as a piece of 
consulting work, and should not contain recommendations for the company.  
 
Specific requirements: 
 
No two students can select the same organisation unless specific approval has been given by the 
lecturer – which will only be given if you are intending to work for an organisation that you wish to 
study (choices must be uploaded to the specific forum thread on Moodle, first person to select an 
organisation will be the only one allowed to study it). 
 
All work should be the students own work (see module outline for specific explanation of this point, 
and rules about use of AI), but the use and appropriate citing of multiple other sources of evidence, 
insight or advice is essential (citations using Harvard referencing style only please, 
https://answers.lancaster.ac.uk/display/LLD/Harvard+Referencing ). A good or very good report 
would most likely cite between 50 and 100 separate sources, in order to show a depth of study and 
a level of robust evidence to back up the analysis and the claims you ultimately wish to make. 
 
Usually, we expect students to make the piece non-judgemental and ethically balanced, as an 
independent review and evaluation of the activities and strategies of the firm. 
 
A DIGITAL copy of your review must be uploaded to the specified Moodle space. Note that this is a 
REPORT and not an essay so the document you load up should look like a professional report and 
not like an academic essay or literature review of response to exam-type questions. 
 
  Guidance on task completion: 
 
This coursework is designed to be progressive, and to allow you to put into practice the work we 
complete throughout the lectures, tutorials and case study sessions of this module. 
 
Advice on how to succeed with this coursework will be given continuously, throughout the module, 
and is embedded in all the learning that takes place.  You should ensure that you attend all lectures 
(which are described in your timetable as ‘workshops’) and make a concerted effort to engage in all 
group activities.   
 
In previous years students have said that this coursework has been a highlight of their studies, 
allowing them great freedom, but also placing them under new forms of intellectual pressure.  For 
these reasons you are strongly advised to begin immediately, and not stop working on this, bit by 
bit, every week until the deadline for submission. 
 
 
Guidance on developing a high quality report 
 
▪ Each piece of analysis within your report needs to try to explain something, some aspect of 
the overall situation you are exploring.  In doing this it must draw on multiple sources of data 
– you cannot make a statement of fact (eg this is a very big company) without it having some 
evidence to back it up. 
▪ Statements you make need to be specific and related to clear evidence. For example, do not 
say “this is a global firm” and include no citations – you should say “this firm operates in 87 
countries across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia and Australasia  employing around 
120,000 people” and this is then followed by cites to show where your data came from.  
▪ The models we have available to us should be used to help us better understand the 
situation.  You need to know the models very well indeed in order to use them properly.  The 
lecture notes/slides are insufficient – they simply highlight the key places to start looking.  
The readings on Moodle are critical to allowing you to fully understand, then apply, the 
models.  Further self-study and self-search for additional resources and explanations or 
examples of how the models are used in practice is recommended. 
▪ Do not try to use too many different theories or models – each one you apply needs to be 
well utilised, with good data, good analysis, and sensible discussion of what you know once 
you have applied it to a situation: what do you now understand, or what can you now explain 
in a more analytical or insightful way?  This naturally takes up a lot of space, so expect to use 
1-3 models or frameworks, then take care to draw the insights together in a well-argued 
conclusion. 
▪ In practice this approach means you need lots of sources, ideally many different sources, to 
support your assignment.  Good assignments tend to have between 50 and 100 separate  references in them. These should also be diverse, and not reliant too much on the company’s 
own websites or documents. 
▪ The report needs to look like a report, not an essay.  This is important as it allows you to be 
creative in terms of the use of charts, graphics, and so on without that impacting on word 
count.  It also allows you to emphasise key points, and encourages you to write clearly and 
develop short, neat sentences.  The best way to get examples of report styles is by googling 
“Think tank” or “London Think Tank” and looking at the reporting styles of these institutions.   
▪ You are strongly advised to read the writing guides posted on Moodle before you write too 
much, or while you do your editing.  In the past, many students have lost marks because of 
poor English grammar. There are learning services available in LUMS to help you with your 
writing – these are not only for international students, they are for everyone.  But these are 
not proof reading services that you use at the end of your work, these are learning services 
that you should be talking to by the 2nd or 3rd week of term, to start sharing your writing with 
them and getting support to improve. 
▪ There are no specific ways to approach this assignment.  The key question to ask yourself 
when you review your own work is: have I created a clear, believable and thorough piece of 
work that allows the reader to better understand a complex ethical situation?  
▪ Make a start as soon as you can, but do not feel that you need to start at the beginning.  Do a 
bit of analysis – something that might sit in the middle of your report – then think about what 
needs to go in front of it or behind it.   
These are the headlines for the marking grid we use, and some of the questions we ask ourselves as 
we look at your work.  Note that this is NOT a definitive guide to the marking process, but should 
give you a clue about what elements need to be included in a good submission: 
 
 
▪ Structure & Presentation  
o Is the ethical problem and perspective clearly set up in the introduction? 
o What is the quality of visual presentation and overall style of the report? 
o What is the quality of English throughout the report? 
o Is the report well structured, to give a logical flow to the ideas? 
 
▪ Sources  
o How good do the sources look –  diverse, well selected, not just reliant on company 
materials?  
o Have the choices been justified, and judiciously used to construct arguments - are 
there evidence gaps? 
o If academic references are used, are they appropriate and accurately used? 
  ▪ Theories  
o Which theories are being used here - is it a good cross section from the course? 
o Do they seem like the best choices for the intended analysis? 
o How well are they used to study the situation, and go beyond mere description? 
o Is data used well in the theories, or are assumptions/unjustified statements made? 
o Does the theory require more or different evidence, or does it give a sense of 
reliability and completeness? 
 
▪ Argument & Insight  
o Are the outputs from theoretical analysis discussed and conclusions drawn? 
o Are these ideas and outputs well combined to build the bigger argument or insight? 
o Is the flow of these arguments logical and well-constructed? 
o How compelling are the points being made? 
o Does the flow of argument and evidence follow appropriately from the initial setup 
in the intro? 
o How original or insightful are the ideas being developed? 
 
▪ Conclusions and Summary 
o How well is everything brought together in the conclusion? 
o Are key points made and presented in a way suitable to the intended audience? 
o Do statements follow on from the data/analysis/argument or go beyond them? 
o Is there any creativity in the insights being drawn out, do they show original 
thinking? 
o Is the executive summary at the front of the document presented clearly and briefly? 
o Does the executive summary reflect – but not exceed – the contents of the main 
report, highlighting key aspects from the entire document?

Psychologists have long identified that the way we perceive events is biased and depends on whether the 
outcome is positive or negative. Positive outcomes tend to be attributed internally, to our own skills and 
capabilities, whereas negative outcomes tend to be attributed to external factors. In other words, when it goes 
wrong you look to blame someone, or something, else. This idea is called Locus of Control [LOC]. There is 
also a link between locus of control and deceptive behaviours, when individuals justify deception due to 
external factors. 
 
You are encouraged to take responsibility for what happened. If your poor performance was due to low 
levels of effort, commitment and/or preparation, then you must reflect on why you didn’t put the effort in and 
why you didn’t try to succeed in the game. Did you think it would be easy? Are you afraid to try and fail? Did 
you ‘settle’? Consider some background reading on the concept of anti-fragility. 
 
This links to a second psychological bias, that of Confirmation Bias. This is where you pick evidence that 
suits your position and ignore/undervalue/dismiss anything that might contradict it. It’s easy to confirm your 
position/attitude/belief, if you never let anything in that would undermine it. 
 
A third psychological mechanism that may be relevant relates to deception, and the tendency to think in one 
way then act in an opposing way. This is called Cognitive Dissonance. An example of this might be to say 
you want an ‘open and honest’ dialogue but then introduce misinformation into the game and act deceptively. 
Another example would be to say you want ‘collaborate’ then behave in your own self-interest. These are not 
compatible positions. People who experience dissonance often try to justify it with unusual or irrational 
reasons or ‘cherry pick’ the evidence to suit their position (again, confirmation bias). 
 
When reflecting on the events in the game – and trying to learn from it – it is essential that you are honest, 
open-minded, robust, creative and insightful about the real reasons behind the way things turned out the way 
they did. That’s not to say that luck doesn’t play a part…. but there is good luck as well as bad.
